zh: 菩提樹東渡尼連禪那河，大林中有窣堵波。其北有池，香象侍母處也。如來在昔修菩薩行，為香象子，居北山中，遊此池側。其母盲也，採藕根，汲清水，恭行孝養，與時推移。屬有一人，遊林迷路，彷徨往來，悲號慟哭。象子聞而愍焉，導之以示歸路。是人既還，遂白王曰：「我知香象遊舍林藪，此奇貨也，可往捕之。」王納其言，興兵往狩，是人前導，指象示王，即時兩臂墮落，若有斬截者。其王雖驚此異，仍縛象子以歸。象子既已維縶多時，而不食水草，典廐者以聞，王遂親問之。象子曰：「我母盲冥，累日飢餓，今見幽厄，詎能甘食？」王愍其情也，故遂放之。其側窣堵波，前建石柱，是昔迦葉波佛於此宴坐。其側有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。
en_current: East of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree, crossing the Nairañjanā River, there is a stūpa in a great forest. To its north is a pond, which is the place where a fragrant elephant (gandhahastin) attended to his mother. In the past, when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he was a young fragrant elephant living in the northern mountains, who would roam by the side of this pond. His mother was blind, and he would gather lotus roots and draw clear water, respectfully performing his filial duties and adapting to the changing seasons. It happened that a man, wandering in the forest and losing his way, paced back and forth, wailing and crying in distress. The young elephant heard him and, feeling compassion, guided him to show him the way home. Once the man had returned, he reported to the king, saying, "I know of a fragrant elephant wandering in the forest thickets; this is a rare treasure, and you may go to capture it." The king accepted his words and raised an army to go hunting. The man acted as a guide, but the moment he pointed out the elephant to the king, both his arms fell off as if they had been severed. Although the king was startled by this strange event, he still bound the young elephant and brought him back. After the young elephant had been tied up for a long time, he would not eat grass or drink water. The stable keeper reported this to the king, who then went in person to question him. The young elephant said, "My mother is blind and has been starving for days; now that I am suffering in captivity, how could I find food sweet?" The king, feeling compassion for his situation, released him. Beside this is a stūpa, with a stone pillar erected in front, which is the place where the Buddha Kāśyapa (迦葉波佛) once sat in meditation. Nearby are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

zh: 四佛坐東渡莫訶河，至大林中，有石柱，是外道入定發惡願處。昔有外道欝頭藍子者，志逸煙霞，身遺草澤，於此法林栖神匿迹。既具五神通，得第一有定。摩揭陀王特深宗敬，每至中時，請就宮食。欝頭藍子凌虛履空，往來無替。摩揭陀王候時瞻望，亦既至已，捧接置座。王將出遊，欲委留事，簡擢中宮，無堪承命。有少息女，淑慎令儀，既親且賢，無出其右，摩揭陀王召而命曰：「吾方遠遊，將有所委，爾宜悉心，慎終其事。彼欝頭藍仙，宿所宗敬，時至來飯，如我所奉。」勅誡既已，便即巡覽。少女承旨，瞻候如儀，大仙至已，捧而置座。欝頭藍子既觸女人，起欲界染，退失神通，飯訖言歸，不得虛遊。中心愧恥，詭謂女曰：「吾比修道業，入定怡神，凌虛往來，略無暇景，國人願覩，聞之久矣。然先達垂訓，利物為務，豈守獨善，忘其兼濟？今欲從門而出，履地而往，使夫覩見之徒，咸蒙福利。」王女聞已，宣告遠近。是時人以馳競，灑掃衢路，百千萬眾，佇望來儀。欝頭藍子步自王宮，至彼法林，宴坐入定，心馳外境，棲林則烏鳥嚶囀，臨池乃魚鼈諠聲，情散心亂，失神廢定。乃生忿恚，即發惡願：「願我當來為暴惡獸，狸身鳥翼，搏食生類，身廣三千里，兩翅各廣千五百里，投林噉諸羽族，入流食彼水生。」發願既已，忿心漸息，勤求頃之，復得本定。不久命終，生第一有天，壽八萬劫。如來記之，天壽畢已，當果昔願，得此弊身。從是流轉惡道，未期出離。
en_current: To the east of where the four Buddhas sat, one crosses the Mahā (莫訶河) River and arrives in a great forest, where there is a stone pillar; this is the place where a non-Buddhist practitioner entered into meditation and made an evil vow. In the past, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子), whose aspirations transcended the mists and clouds, and whose body abandoned the marshes and thickets; he dwelt in this forest of the Dharma, hiding his spirit and concealing his traces. Having attained the five supernatural powers, he achieved the meditation of the peak of existence (bhavāgra). The King of Magadha (摩揭陀王) held him in particularly deep respect and, every day at noon, invited him to the palace for a meal. Udraka Rāmaputra would soar through the void and walk upon the air, coming and going without fail. The King of Magadha would watch and wait for the appointed time; once he arrived, the king would personally receive him and escort him to his seat.  When the king was about to depart on a tour and wished to entrust his affairs to someone, he examined those in the inner palace, but found no one capable of undertaking the command. He had a young daughter of virtuous and prudent character; she was both close to him and wise, with none surpassing her, so the King of Magadha summoned her and commanded: "I am about to travel far and have something to entrust to you; you should be diligent and see this matter through to the end with care. That immortal Udraka Rāmaputra is one whom I have long held in respect; when the time comes for him to arrive for his meal, treat him just as I have done."  Having given these instructions, the king departed on his tour. The young lady accepted the command and waited upon him according to the rites; when the great immortal arrived, she supported him and assisted him to his seat. Once Udraka Rāmaputra had touched the woman, desire for the realm of sense-objects arose, and he regressed, losing his supernatural powers. When he had finished his meal and spoke of returning, he was unable to soar through the void. Feeling ashamed and humiliated in his heart, he deceitfully said to the woman: "I have recently been cultivating the path, entering into meditation to soothe my spirit, and have been soaring through the void to come and go, having almost no leisure time. I have long heard that the people of the country wish to see this. However, the sages of old have left us instructions that benefiting others is our primary duty; how could I remain content with my own virtue and forget the need to assist others? I now wish to depart through the gate and travel by treading upon the ground, so that all those who see me may receive blessings and benefit." Having heard this, the king’s daughter made the announcement far and near. At that time, people rushed to compete, sweeping and cleaning the roads, and hundreds of thousands of people stood waiting to see his arrival. Udraka Rāmaputra (欝頭藍子) walked from the royal palace to that religious forest and sat in meditation, but his mind wandered to external environments; when he stayed in the forest, the birds chirped, and when he approached the pond, the fish and turtles made noise, so that his feelings were distracted and his mind disturbed, causing him to lose his concentration and abandon his meditation. He then gave rise to anger and immediately made an evil vow: "May I in the future become a fierce and wicked beast with the body of a wildcat and the wings of a bird to seize and eat living creatures; let my body be three thousand li wide, with two wings each fifteen hundred li wide, so that I may enter the forests to devour the feathered tribes and enter the currents to eat the aquatic beings." Having made this vow, his anger gradually subsided, and after practicing diligently for a while, he regained his original concentration. Not long after, he passed away and was born in the Heaven of the First Existence (第一有天), with a lifespan of eighty thousand kalpas. The Tathāgata predicted that once his heavenly lifespan was exhausted, he would fulfill his former vow and obtain this wretched body. From that point on, he would wander through the evil paths, with no time set for his liberation.

zh: 四佛坐東渡莫訶河，至大林中，有石柱，是外道入定發惡願處。
en_current: To the east of the seats of the four Buddhas, one crosses the Mahā River and arrives in a great forest where there is a stone pillar; this is the place where a non-Buddhist entered into meditative concentration and made an evil vow.

name_zh: 屈屈吒播陀山 (窶盧播陀山)
zh: 莫訶河東入大林野，行百餘里，至屈屈（居勿反）吒播陀山（唐言雞足），亦謂窶盧播陀山（唐言尊足）。高巒陗，無極深，壑洞無涯，山麓谿㵎，喬林羅谷，岡岑嶺嶂，繁草被巖，峻起三峯，傍挺絕崿，氣將天接，形與雲同。其後尊者大迦葉波居中寂滅，不敢指言，故云尊足。摩訶迦葉波者，聲聞弟子也，得六神通，具八解脫。如來化緣斯畢，垂將涅槃，告迦葉波曰：「我於曠劫勤修苦行，為諸眾生求無上法，昔所願期，今已果滿。我今將欲入大涅槃，以諸法藏囑累於汝，住持宣布，勿有失墜。姨母所獻金縷袈裟，慈氏成佛，留以傳付。我遺法中諸修行者，若比丘、比丘尼、鄔波索迦、（唐言近事男。舊曰伊蒱塞，又曰優波塞，又曰優婆塞，皆訛也）、鄔波斯迦（唐言近事女。舊曰優婆斯，又曰優婆夷，皆訛也），皆先濟渡，令離流轉。」迦葉承旨，住持正法。結集既已，至第二十年，厭世無常，將入寂滅。乃往雞足山，山陰而上，屈盤取路，至西南岡。山峯險阻，崖徑槃薄，乃以錫扣，剖之如割。山徑既開，逐路而進，槃紆曲折，迴互斜通，至于山頂，東北面出，既入三峯之中，捧佛袈裟而立，以願力故，三峯斂覆，故今此山三脊隆起。當來慈氏世尊之興世也，三會說法之後，餘有無量憍慢眾生，將登此山，至迦葉所。慈氏彈指，山峯自開，彼諸眾生既見迦葉，更增憍慢。時大迦葉授衣致辭，禮敬已畢，身昇虛空，示諸神變，化火焚身，遂入寂滅。時眾瞻仰，憍慢心除，因而感悟，皆證聖果。故今山上建窣堵波，靜夜遠望，或見明炬，及有登山，遂無所覩。
en_current: Going east from the Mahā River, one enters a great forest wilderness and, after traveling over a hundred li, reaches Kukkuṭapāda Mountain (屈屈吒播陀山) (屈 pronounced 居勿反) (translated into Chinese as Jizu, "Cock's Foot"), also called Gurupāda Mountain (translated into Chinese as Zunzu, "Venerable Foot"). The high peaks are steep and the ravines infinitely deep; the caverns are boundless, and at the foot of the mountain by the mountain streams, tall trees fill the valleys, while ridges and cliffs are covered with lush grass. Three peaks rise sharply with sheer precipices standing at their sides, their atmosphere joining with the heavens and their forms merging with the clouds. Because the Venerable Mahākāśyapa later entered nirvana in its midst, people did not dare to refer to him directly by name, and thus it is called "Venerable Foot."  Mahākāśyapa (摩訶迦葉波) is a disciple of the Śrāvaka vehicle who attained the six supernatural powers and possesses the eight liberations. When the Tathāgata had finished his work of transformation and was about to enter nirvana, he told Kāśyapa: "Throughout vast eons I have diligently practiced austerities, seeking the supreme Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings. The vows I made in the past have now been fulfilled. I am now about to enter the great nirvana, and I entrust the entire treasury of the Dharma to you. Maintain and proclaim it; do not let it be lost or fall into ruin. The golden-threaded robe offered by my aunt is to be kept and passed on to Maitreya when he attains buddhahood. Among the practitioners within my bequeathed Dharma—whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣunīs, upāsakas (鄔波索迦) (in the Tang language, 'laymen who serve'; formerly called yipusai 伊蒱塞, also youposai 優波塞, also youposai 優婆塞, all of which are erroneous), or upāsikās (鄔波斯迦) (in the Tang language, 'laywomen who serve'; formerly called youposi 優婆斯, also youpoyi 優婆夷, all of which are erroneous)—all of them are to be liberated first, causing them to depart from the cycle of transmigration." Kāśyapa accepted the command to uphold the True Dharma. Once the compilation was finished, in the twentieth year, he grew weary of the world and its impermanence and was about to enter final extinction. He then went to Mount Kukkutapāda (雞足山), ascended from the northern side of the mountain, and took a winding path to the southwest ridge. The mountain peaks were steep and obstructed, and the cliff paths were rugged; he struck them with his staff, and they split open as if cut. Once the mountain path was opened, he proceeded along the way, winding and turning through crisscrossing passages until he reached the summit and emerged on the northeast side. Having entered the midst of the three peaks, he stood holding the Buddha’s robe, and by the power of his vow, the three peaks closed over him, which is why the mountain now has three protruding ridges. When the future Maitreya, the World-Honored One, appears in the world and completes his three assemblies of preaching the Dharma, there will remain countless arrogant sentient beings who shall ascend this mountain and come to the place of Kāśyapa. When Maitreya snaps his fingers, the mountain peaks will open of their own accord; yet when those sentient beings see Kāśyapa, their arrogance will increase even further. At that time, the Great Kāśyapa will present the robe and deliver a discourse; once they have finished paying their respects, he will ascend into the void, manifest various spiritual transformations, transform into fire to consume his body, and thus enter final extinction. At that time, the assembly will gaze up in reverence, their arrogant minds will be dispelled, and through this realization, they will all attain the holy fruits. Therefore, a stūpa has been built on the mountain; on quiet nights, one may see a bright torch from afar, but upon ascending the mountain, nothing can be seen.

zh: 鷄足山東北行百餘里，至佛陀伐那山。峯崖崇峻，巘崿隱嶙，巖間石室，佛嘗降止。傍有盤石，帝釋、梵王摩牛頭栴檀塗飾如來，今其石上餘香郁烈。五百羅漢潛靈於此，諸有感遇，或得覩見，時作沙彌之形，入里乞食，隱顯靈奇之迹，羌難以述。
en_current: Traveling more than one hundred li northeast from Kukkuṭapāda Mountain (鷄足山), one reaches the mountain of Buddhavana (佛陀伐那山). Its peaks and cliffs are lofty and steep, with jagged and towering ridges; among the rocks is a stone chamber where the Buddha once descended and stayed. Beside it is a flat rock where Śakra (帝釋) and the Brahmā King (梵王) ground ox-head sandalwood to anoint the Tathāgata; even now, a strong fragrance remains upon the stone. Five hundred arhats conceal their spirits here, and those who have a spiritual resonance may sometimes see them; they occasionally take the form of śrāmaṇeras to enter villages and beg for food, and their miraculous traces, appearing and disappearing, are truly difficult to describe.

zh: 佛陀伐那山空谷中東行三十餘里，至洩（移結反）瑟知林（唐言杖林）。林竹修篠，被山滿谷。其先有婆羅門，聞釋迦佛身長丈六，常懷疑惑，未之信也，乃以丈六竹杖，欲量佛身。恒於杖端出過丈六，如是增高，莫能窮實，遂投杖而去，因植根焉。中有大窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。如來在昔，於此七日為諸天、人現大神通，說深妙法。杖林中近有鄔波索迦闍耶犀那者（唐言勝軍），西印度剎帝利種也，志尚夷簡，情悅山林，迹居幻境，心遊真際，內外典籍，窮究幽微，辭論清高，儀範閑雅。諸沙門、婆羅門、外道、異學、國王、大臣、長者、豪右，相趨通謁，伏膺請益。受業門人，十室而六。年漸七十，耽讀不倦，餘藝捐廢，唯習佛經，策勵身心，不舍晝夜。印度之法，香末為泥，作小窣堵波，高五六寸，書寫經文，以置其中，謂之法舍利也；數漸盈積，建大窣堵波，總聚於內，常修供養。故勝軍之為業也，口則宣說妙法，導誘學人，手乃作窣堵波，式崇勝福，夜又經行禮誦，宴坐思惟，寢食不遑，晝夜無怠。年百歲矣，志業不衰。三十年間，凡作七拘胝（唐言億）法舍利窣堵波。每滿一拘胝，建大窣堵波，而總置中，盛修供養，請諸僧眾，法會稱慶，其時神光燭曜，靈異昭彰，自茲厥後，時放光明。
en_current: Traveling more than thirty *li* eastward through the empty valleys of Buddhavana Mountain (Skt. *buddha-vana*), one reaches Yaṣṭivana (洩瑟知林) (洩 is pronounced y[i] + [j]ie) (in the language of Tang, this means "Staff Forest"). The forest’s bamboo is tall and slender, covering the mountains and filling the valleys. Long ago, there was a Brahmin who heard that the body of the Buddha Śākyamuni was sixteen feet tall; he constantly harbored doubts and, unable to believe it, took a sixteen-foot bamboo staff, intending to measure the Buddha’s body. The staff always extended beyond the sixteen-foot mark at its tip; as it continued to grow taller in this way, he could never reach the truth of it, so he threw the staff away and departed, and it subsequently took root. Within the forest is a large *stūpa* built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here manifesting great supernatural powers for the sake of gods and humans, and expounding the profound and subtle Dharma.  Recently, in the Staff Forest, there was an *upāsaka* named Jayasena (in the language of Tang, this means "Victorious Army"), who belonged to the Kṣatriya caste of Western India. His aspirations were for simplicity and ease, his heart delighted in the mountains and forests, and while his physical traces remained in this illusory realm, his mind roamed the boundaries of ultimate truth. He had thoroughly investigated the subtle mysteries of both internal and external scriptures, possessing noble eloquence and elegant manners. Śramaṇas, Brahmins, followers of non-Buddhist paths, heterodox scholars, kings, ministers, elders, and the wealthy and influential all flocked to visit him, bowing their heads to request instruction. Of every ten households, six had sent disciples to receive his instruction. Now approaching seventy years of age, he studied with tireless devotion; having abandoned all other arts, he practiced only the Buddhist scriptures, exerting his body and mind without ceasing day or night. According to the custom of India, scented powder is mixed into clay to make small stupas five or six inches high; scriptures are written and placed inside them, which are called Dharma relics. As the number gradually accumulates, a large stupa is built to house them all within, where offerings are constantly performed. Thus, the practice of Jayasena (勝軍) was as follows: his mouth would proclaim the wonderful Dharma to guide and encourage students, while his hands would make stupas to cultivate superior merit. At night, he would practice circumambulation, chanting, and seated meditation, never finding time for sleep or food, and working day and night without slackening. He reached one hundred years of age, yet his resolve and work did not decline. Over a period of thirty years, he made a total of seven koṭis (in the Tang language, *yi* [億]) of Dharma-relic stupas. Each time he completed one koṭi, he built a large stupa to house them all, where he grandly performed offerings and invited the monastic assembly to celebrate with a religious ceremony. At those times, a divine light would shine brilliantly as a manifest miracle, and from then on, it would emit light from time to time.

zh: 杖林西南十餘里，大山陽，有二溫泉，其水甚熱。在昔如來化出此水，於中浴焉。今者尚存，清流無減，遠近之人，皆來就浴，沈痾宿疹，無不除差。其傍則有窣堵波，如來經行之處也。
en_current: More than ten *li* to the southwest of the Stick Wood (Yaṣṭivana), on the southern slope of a great mountain, there are two hot springs, the water of which is extremely hot. In the past, the Tathāgata manifested this water and bathed therein. They still exist today with their clear flow undiminished; people from near and far all come to bathe in them, and there are none among those with chronic illnesses or old ailments who are not cured. Beside them is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Tathāgata once walked.

zh: 杖林東南行六七里，至大山，橫嶺之前有石窣堵波，昔如來兩三月為諸人、天於此說法，時頻毘娑羅王欲來聽法，乃疏山積石，壘階以進，廣二十餘步，長三四里。
en_current: Traveling six or seven li southeast from the Yaṣṭi Wood (杖林), one reaches a great mountain. In front of a transverse ridge stands a stone stupa where the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma to humans and devas for two or three months. At that time, King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王), wishing to come and hear the Dharma, cleared the mountain and piled up stones to build a staircase for his ascent, measuring over twenty paces in width and three or four li in length.

zh: 大山北三四里，有孤山，昔廣博仙人棲隱於此，鑿崖為室，餘趾尚存，傳教門人，遺風猶扇。
en_current: Three or four li to the north of the great mountain is an isolated hill (孤山), where in the past the Rishi Vyāsa (廣博仙人) lived in seclusion. He chiseled into the cliff to create a chamber, the remains of which still exist. He transmitted his teachings to his disciples, and his legacy still prevails.

name_zh: 小孤山 (石室・阿素洛宮)
zh: 孤山東北四五里，有小孤山，山壁石室廣袤可坐千餘人矣，如來在昔於此三月說法。石室上有大磐石，帝釋、梵王摩牛頭栴檀塗飾佛身，石上餘香，于今郁烈。石室西南隅有巖岫，印度謂之阿素洛（舊曰阿修羅，又曰阿須倫，又曰阿修羅，皆訛也）宮也。往有好事者，深閑呪術，顧儔命侶，十有四人，約契同志，入此巖岫。行三四十里，廓然大明，乃見城邑臺觀，皆是金銀琉璃。是人至已，有諸少女佇立門側，歡喜迎接，甚加禮遇。於是漸進至內城門，有二婢使各捧金盤，盛滿花香，而來迎候。謂諸人曰：「宜就池浴，塗冠香花，已而後入，斯為美矣。唯彼術士，宜時速進。」餘十三人遂即沐浴，既入池已，恍若有忘，乃坐稻田中，去此之北平川中，已三四十里矣。石室側有棧道，廣十餘步，長四五里。昔頻毘娑羅王將往佛所，乃斬石通谷，疏崖填川，或壘石，或鑿巖，作為階級，以至佛所。
en_current: Four or five li to the northeast of the Isolated Hill is the Small Isolated Hill. In the cliffside of the mountain is a stone chamber, vast and spacious, capable of seating over a thousand people; here the Tathāgata in the past preached the Dharma for three months. Above the stone chamber is a large flat rock where Śakra and Brahmā ground ox-head sandalwood to anoint the Buddha’s body; the lingering fragrance on the rock remains potent to this day. In the southwest corner of the stone chamber is a rocky grotto, which in India is called the palace of the *asura* (阿素洛) (formerly called *axiuluo* [阿修羅], also *axulun* [阿須倫], also *axiuluo*; all are erroneous). In the past, there was a curious man, deeply skilled in spells, who gathered companions, fourteen people in all, and having made a pact to share the same purpose, entered this grotto. After traveling thirty or forty li, it suddenly became brightly illuminated, and they beheld cities, towers, and pavilions, all made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli. Once these people arrived, there were various young maidens standing by the gates who joyfully welcomed them and treated them with great courtesy. Proceeding gradually to the inner city gate, there were two maidservants, each holding a golden basin filled with flowers and incense, who came to greet them. They said to the group, "It is fitting to go to the pool to bathe, to apply perfumes and wear flower garlands, and only after that to enter; this would be most excellent. Only that sorcerer should proceed quickly." The other thirteen people then bathed, but as soon as they entered the pool, they felt as if they had forgotten everything, and they found themselves sitting in a rice paddy on a level plain to the north of this place, already thirty or forty li away. Beside the stone chamber is a plank road, more than ten paces wide and four or five li long. In the past, when King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) was about to go to the place of the Buddha, he had rocks cut to open the valley and cliffs leveled to fill the ravines; he either piled up stones or excavated the cliffs to create steps, in order to reach the place of the Buddha.

name_zh: 矩奢掲羅補羅城 (上茅宮城)
zh: 從此大山中東行六十餘里，至矩奢揭羅補羅城（唐言上茅宮城）。上茅宮城，摩揭陀國之正中，古先君王之所都，多出勝上吉祥香茅，以故謂之上茅城也。崇山四周，以為外郭，西通峽徑，北闢山門，東西長，南北狹，周一百五十餘里。內城餘趾周三十餘里。羯尼迦樹遍諸蹊徑，花含殊馥，色爛黃金，暮春之月，林皆金色。宮城北門外有窣堵波，是提婆達多與未生怨王共為親友，乃放護財醉象，欲害如來。如來指端出五師子，醉象於此馴伏而前。伏醉象東北有窣堵波，是舍利子聞阿濕婆恃比丘（唐言馬勝）說法證果之處。初，舍利子在家也，高才雅量，見重當時，門生學徒，傳以受業。此時將入王舍大城，馬勝比丘亦方乞食。時舍利子遙見馬勝，謂門生曰：「彼來者甚庠序，不證聖果，豈斯調寂？宜少佇待，觀其進趣。」馬勝比丘已證羅漢，心得自在，容止和雅，振錫來儀。舍利子曰：「長老善安樂耶？師何人，證何法，若此之悅豫乎？」馬勝謂曰：「爾不知耶，淨飯王太子，捨轉輪王位，悲愍六趣，苦行六年，證三菩提，具一切智，是吾師也。夫法者，非有非空，難用銓緒，唯佛與佛乃能究述，豈伊愚昧所能詳議？」因為頌說，稱讚佛法。舍利子聞已，便獲果證。舍利子證果北不遠，有大深坑，傍建窣堵波，是室利毱多（唐言勝密）以火坑、毒飯欲害佛處。勝密者，宗信外道，深著邪見。諸梵志曰：「喬答摩國人尊敬，遂令我徒無所恃賴，汝今可請至家飯會，門穿大坑，滿中縱火，棧以朽木，覆以燥土。凡諸飲食，皆雜毒藥，若免火坑，當遭毒食。」勝密承命，便設毒會。城中之人皆知勝密於世尊所起惡害心，咸皆勸請，願佛勿往。世尊告曰：「無得懷憂。如來之身，物莫能害。」於是受請而往。足履門閫，火坑成池，清瀾澄鑒，蓮花彌漫。勝密見已，憂惶無措，謂其徒曰：「以術免火，尚有毒食。」世尊飯食已訖，為說妙法，勝密聞已，謝咎歸依。
en_current: Traveling east from these great mountains for more than sixty li, one reaches the city of Kuśāgrapura (矩奢揭羅補羅城; in the language of Tang, the City of Superior Thatch Palaces). The City of Superior Thatch Palaces is located in the center of the kingdom of Magadha and was the capital of ancient kings; because it produces an abundance of excellent and auspicious fragrant thatch, it is called the City of Superior Thatch. Lofty mountains surround it, serving as an outer wall; to the west it connects to a mountain pass, and to the north a mountain gate opens. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south, with a circumference of more than one hundred and fifty li. The remaining foundations of the inner city measure more than thirty li in circumference. *Karṇikāra* (羯尼迦) trees cover all the paths; their flowers contain a unique fragrance and their color is as brilliant as gold, so that in the month of late spring, the forests are all golden.  Outside the north gate of the palace city is a stūpa, marking the place where Devadatta, having become an intimate friend of King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王), released the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla (護財) in an attempt to harm the Tathāgata. From the tips of the Tathāgata’s fingers, five lions emerged, and the intoxicated elephant was subdued and bowed down here. To the northeast of the place where the intoxicated elephant was subdued is a stūpa, marking the place where Śāriputra heard the bhikṣu Aśvajit (阿濕婆恃) (in the language of Tang, "Horse Victory" [馬勝]) preach the Dharma and attained the fruit of sainthood.   Formerly, when Śāriputra was a householder, he possessed high talent and elegant bearing, and was esteemed by his contemporaries; students and disciples came to him to receive instruction. At this time, he was about to enter the great city of Rājagṛha, and the bhikṣu Aśvajit was also just then begging for food. At that time, Śāriputra saw Aśvajit from afar and said to his disciples, "That person coming here is very composed and dignified; if he has not attained the holy fruit, how could he be so calm and tranquil?" "We should wait a moment and observe his demeanor." The bhikṣu Aśvajit had already attained the state of an arhat; his mind was at ease, his bearing was gentle and refined, and he approached with the ringing of his khakkhara. Śāriputra said, "Elder, are you well and at peace? Who is your teacher, and what Dharma have you realized, that you are so joyful?" Aśvajit replied, "Do you not know? The crown prince of King Śuddhodana, who renounced the position of a wheel-turning monarch, out of compassion for the six destinies, practiced austerities for six years, realized perfect enlightenment (*saṃbodhi*), and possesses omniscience—he is my teacher. As for the Dharma, it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is difficult to define or explain. Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully describe it; how could one as ignorant as I discuss it in detail?" He then recited a verse in praise of the Buddha’s Dharma. Upon hearing this, Śāriputra attained the fruit.  Not far to the north of where Śāriputra attained the fruit, there is a large, deep pit with a stūpa built beside it; this is the place where Śrīgupta (室利毱多) (in the language of Tang, "Victorious Secret" [勝密]) attempted to harm the Buddha with a fire pit and poisoned food. This Śrīgupta followed the teachings of the non-Buddhists and was deeply attached to erroneous views. The various Brahmins said to him, "Gautama is respected by the people of the country, which has left our followers with nothing to rely on. You should now invite him to your home for a feast; dig a large pit at the gate, fill it with fire, bridge it with rotten wood, and cover it with dry earth. All the food and drink should be mixed with poison; if he escapes the fire pit, he will surely encounter the poisoned food." Śrīgupta accepted their command and prepared the poisoned feast. The people in the city all knew that Śrīgupta (勝密) harbored evil and harmful intentions toward the World-Honored One, and they all urged and pleaded with the Buddha not to go. The World-Honored One replied, "Do not harbor anxiety. The body of the Tathāgata cannot be harmed by anything." Thereupon, he accepted the invitation and went. As his foot stepped upon the threshold of the gate, the fire pit turned into a pool, its clear waters reflecting like a mirror and filled with blooming lotuses. Having seen this, Śrīgupta was filled with panic and confusion, and said to his disciples, "He used magic to escape the fire, but there is still the poisoned food." After the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he preached the wonderful Dharma for him; having heard this, Śrīgupta confessed his faults and took refuge.

name_zh: 時縛迦說法堂 (菴婆羅園)
zh: 勝密火坑東北，山城之曲，有窣堵波，是時縛迦大醫（舊曰耆婆，訛也）於此為佛建說法堂，周其壖垣種植花菓，餘趾蘖株尚有遺迹。如來在世，多於中止。其傍復有縛迦故宅，餘基舊井，墟坎猶存。
en_current: To the northeast of the fire pit of Śrīgupta (勝密), at a bend in the mountain city, there is a stūpa. This is where the great physician Jīvaka (時縛迦; formerly called Qipo [耆婆], which is incorrect) built a preaching hall for the Buddha. He planted flowers and fruit trees around its surrounding walls, and the remains of the foundations and the stumps of the trees can still be seen. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he often stayed here. Beside it are the former residence of Jīvaka, the remains of the foundations, an old well, and the hollows of the ruins, which still exist.

zh: 宮城東北行十四五里，至姞栗陀羅矩吒山（唐言鷲峯，亦謂鷲臺。舊曰耆闍崛山，訛也）。接北山之陽，孤摽特起，既棲鷲鳥，又類高臺，空翠相映，濃淡分色。如來御世垂五十年，多居此山，廣說妙法。頻毘娑羅王為聞法故，興發人徒，自山麓至峯岑，跨谷凌巖，編石為階，廣十餘步，長五六里。中路有二小窣堵波，一謂下乘，即王至此徒行以進；一謂退凡，即簡凡人不令同往。其山頂則東西長，南北狹。
en_current: Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* northeast from the palace city, one reaches Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain (in the language of Tang, this means Vulture Peak, and it is also called Vulture Terrace; the old name, Qidujue Mountain, is incorrect). It adjoins the southern slope of the North Mountain and rises solitary and steep; it is a place where vultures dwell and it resembles a lofty terrace, with the verdant peaks reflecting against the sky in varying shades of color. For nearly fifty years, while the Tathāgata presided over the world, he resided mostly on this mountain, extensively expounding the subtle Dharma. For the sake of hearing the Dharma, King Bimbisāra mobilized laborers to build a path from the foot of the mountain to the summit, spanning valleys and scaling rocks, laying stones to form steps more than ten paces wide and five or six *li* in length. Midway along the path are two small stūpas: one is called "Dismounting," marking the spot where the king would proceed on foot; the other is called "Turning Back the Ordinary," marking the spot where he would screen out ordinary people and not allow them to accompany him further. The summit of the mountain is long from east to west and narrow from north to south.

zh: 臨崖西埵有甎精舍，高廣奇製，東闢其戶，如來在昔多居說法，今作說法之像，量等如來之身。精舍東有長石，如來經行所履也。傍有大石，高丈四五尺，周三十餘步，是提婆達多遙擲擊佛處也。其南崖下有窣堵波，在昔如來於此說《法花經》。精舍南山崖側有大石室，如來在昔於此入定。佛石室西北，石室前有大磐石，阿難為魔怖處也。尊者阿難於此入定，魔王化作鷲鳥，於黑月夜分據其大石，奮翼驚鳴，以怖尊者。尊者是時驚懼無措，如來鑒見，伸手安慰，通過石壁，摩阿難頂，以大慈言而告之曰：「魔所變化，宜無怖懼。」阿難蒙慰，身心安樂。石上鳥迹、崖中通穴，歲月雖久，于今尚存。精舍側有數石室，舍利子等諸大羅漢於此入定。舍利子石室前有一大井，枯涸無水，墟坎猶存。精舍東北石㵎中有大磐石，是如來曬袈裟之處，衣文明徹，皎如彫刻。其傍石上有佛脚迹，輪文雖暗，規摸可察。北山頂有窣堵波，是如來望摩揭陀城，於此七日說法。
en_current: On the western edge of the cliff stands a brick vihara (精舍), of lofty and spacious, extraordinary construction, with its door opening to the east. In the past, the Tathāgata often resided here to expound the Dharma; today, there is an image of him expounding the Dharma, equal in measure to the body of the Tathāgata. To the east of the vihara is a long stone, which is where the Tathāgata walked during his meditative perambulations. Beside it is a large stone, fourteen or fifteen feet high and over thirty paces in circumference; this is the place where Devadatta threw a rock from afar to strike the Buddha. Below the cliff to the south is a stūpa where, in the past, the Tathāgata expounded the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (法花經). On the side of the mountain cliff to the south of the vihara is a large stone chamber where the Tathāgata entered into meditative concentration in the past. To the northwest of the Buddha’s stone chamber, in front of a cave, is a large flat rock; this is the place where Ānanda was terrified by Māra. While the Venerable Ānanda was in meditative concentration here, the Demon King transformed himself into a vulture; during the dark phase of the moon, it perched upon the large rock, flapping its wings and shrieking to frighten the Venerable One. At that time, the Venerable One was terrified and at a loss. The Tathāgata, perceiving this, reached out his hand to comfort him, passing through the stone wall to stroke Ānanda’s head, and addressed him with words of great compassion: "This is a transformation by Māra; you should have no fear." Having received this comfort, Ānanda’s body and mind became peaceful and joyful. The bird’s tracks on the stone and the hole through the cliff, though much time has passed, still remain today. Beside the vihara are several stone chambers where Śāriputra and other great Arhats entered into meditative concentration. In front of Śāriputra’s stone chamber is a large well; though it is dried up and waterless, its ruins and hollow still remain. In the stony gully to the northeast of the vihara is a large flat rock, which is the place where the Tathāgata dried his kaṣāya; the patterns of the robe are clear and distinct, as bright as if they were carved. Beside it, on the rock, are the footprints of the Buddha; although the wheel markings are faint, their shape and form can still be discerned. On the summit of the north mountain is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata gazed toward the city of Magadha (摩揭陀城) and preached the Dharma for seven days.

zh: 山城北門西有毘布羅山，聞之土俗曰：山西南崖陰，昔有五百溫泉，今者數十而已，然猶有冷有暖，未盡溫也。其泉源發雪山之南無熱惱池，潛流至此，水甚清美，味同本池。流經五百枝小熱地獄，火熱上炎，致斯溫熱。泉流之口，並皆彫石，或作師子、白象之首，或作石筒懸流之道，下乃編石為池。諸方異域咸來此浴，浴者宿疾多差。溫泉左右諸窣堵波及精舍，基址鱗次，並是過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。此處既山水相帶，仁智攸居，隱淪之士蓋亦多矣。
en_current: To the west of the north gate of the mountain city is Mount Vipula (毘布羅山). According to local tradition, on the shaded cliff to the southwest of the mountain, there were formerly five hundred hot springs; today, only several dozen remain, and they are still a mixture of cold and warm, not all of them being hot. The source of these springs originates from Lake Anavatapta (無熱惱池) to the south of the Snowy Mountains (雪山), flowing underground to this location; the water is exceptionally clear and fine, with a taste identical to that of the original lake. The water flows through five hundred branch minor hot hells, where the fiery heat rises upward, causing this warmth. The mouths of the springs are all carved from stone, some fashioned into the heads of lions or white elephants, others forming stone conduits for the cascading water, which flows down into pools constructed of layered stone. People from various regions and foreign lands all come here to bathe, and those who bathe often find their chronic illnesses cured. To the left and right of the hot springs, the foundations of various stūpas and monasteries (精舍) are arranged like fish scales; these are all sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation. Since this place is bordered by mountains and rivers, serving as a dwelling for the benevolent and the wise, there are indeed many recluses living here in seclusion.

zh: 溫泉西有卑鉢羅石室，世尊在昔恒居其中。後壁洞穴是阿素洛宮也。習定比丘多居此室。時出怪異龍、蛇、師子之形，見之者心發狂亂。然斯勝地，靈聖所止，躡迹欽風，忘其災禍。近有比丘，戒行貞潔，心樂幽寂，欲於此室匿迹習定。或有諫曰：「勿往彼也。彼多災異，為害不少，既難取定，亦恐喪身。宜鑒前事，勿貽後悔。」比丘曰：「不然。我方志求佛果，摧伏天魔，若此之害，夫何足言？」便即振錫而往室焉。於是設壇場，誦禁呪。旬日之後，穴出少女，謂比丘曰：「尊者染衣守戒，為含識歸依；修慧習定，作生靈善導。而今居此，驚懼我曹。如來之教，豈若是耶？」比丘曰：「我守淨戒，遵聖教也。匿迹山谷，遠諠雜也。忽此見譏，其咎安在？」對曰：「尊者誦呪聲發，火從外入，燒我居室，苦我枝屬。唯願悲愍，勿復誦呪。」比丘曰：「誦呪自護，非欲害物。往者，行人居此習定，期於聖果，以濟幽塗，覩怪驚懼，喪棄身命，汝之辜也，其何辭乎？」對曰：「罪障既重，智慧斯淺。自今已來，屏居守分，亦願尊者勿誦神呪。」比丘於是修定如初，安靜無害。毘布羅山上有窣堵波，昔者如來說法之處。今有露形外道，多依此住，修習苦行，夙夜匪懈，自旦至昏，旋轉觀察。
en_current: To the west of the hot springs is the Pippala (卑鉢羅) stone cave, where the World-Honored One used to dwell constantly in the past. The cavern in the rear wall is the palace of the Asuras (阿素洛). Many bhikṣus who practice meditation reside in this chamber. At times, strange and monstrous forms of dragons, snakes, and lions appear; those who see them become mentally deranged. However, because this is a superior site where the holy and sagely have dwelt, those who follow in their footsteps and admire their influence forget the disasters and calamities associated with it. Recently, there was a bhikṣu of pure conduct who delighted in quiet seclusion and wished to hide away in this chamber to practice meditation. Someone cautioned him, saying, "Do not go there. It is full of disasters and strange occurrences, causing no small amount of harm. It is difficult to attain concentration there, and I fear you will lose your life. You should take warning from past events and not leave cause for later regret." The bhikṣu replied, "That is not so. I am determined to seek the fruit of Buddhahood and to subdue the heavenly demons; if this is the harm you speak of, how is it worth mentioning?" He then shook his khakkhara-staff and went to the chamber. There, he set up an altar and recited protective mantras. After ten days, a young woman emerged from the cavern and said to the bhikṣu, "Venerable one, you wear the dyed robes and keep the precepts, serving as a refuge for sentient beings; you cultivate wisdom and practice meditation, acting as a virtuous guide for living creatures. Yet now you dwell here and terrify us. Is this the teaching of the Tathāgata?" The bhikṣu replied, "I observe the pure precepts and follow the holy teachings. I hide my tracks in the mountain valleys to stay far from noise and confusion. Why do you suddenly reproach me for this?" She replied, "When you recite your mantras, the sound goes forth, and fire enters from outside, burning my dwelling and afflicting my kin. I only pray that you have compassion and do not recite the mantras again." The bhikṣu said, "I recite the mantras for self-protection, not because I wish to harm living beings. In the past, when practitioners dwelt here to practice meditation, hoping to attain the holy fruit to save those in the dark paths, they saw your monstrosity and were terrified, losing their lives; this was your fault, so what excuse do you have?" She replied, "My karmic obstructions are heavy and my wisdom is shallow. From now on, I shall live in seclusion and keep to my place; I also hope that you, Venerable Sir, will not recite the divine mantras." The bhikṣu then practiced meditation as before, in peace and without harm. On Mount Vipula (毘布羅山) there is a stūpa, the place where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma in the past. Nowadays, many naked heretics (nirgrantha) reside here, practicing austerities without negligence day or night; from dawn until dusk, they turn around and observe the sun.

zh: 山城北門左，南崖陰，東行二三里，至大石室，昔提婆達多於此入定。石室東不遠，磐石上有班采，狀血染，傍建窣堵波，是習定比丘自害證果之處。昔有比丘，勤勵心身，屏居修定，歲月逾遠，不證聖果。退而自咎，竊復歎曰：「無學之果，終不時證；有累之身，徒生何益！」便就此石自刺其頸，是時即證阿羅漢果，上昇虛空，示現神變，化火焚身，而入寂滅。美其雅操，建以記功。比丘證果東石崖上，有石窣堵波，習定比丘投崖證果之處。昔在佛世，有一比丘，宴坐山林，修證果定，精勤已久，不得果證，晝夜繼念，無忘靜定。如來知其根機將發也，遂往彼而成之，自竹林園至山崖下，彈指而召，佇立以待。此比丘遙覩聖眾，身意勇悅，投崖而下，猶其淨心，敬信佛語，未至于地，已獲果證。世尊告曰：「宜知是時。」即昇虛空，示現神變。用彰淨信，故斯封記。
en_current: To the left of the north gate of the mountain city, on the shaded side of the southern cliff, traveling east for two or three li, one arrives at a great stone chamber; in the past, Devadatta entered into meditation here. Not far to the east of the stone chamber, there are colored streaks on a flat rock that appear as if stained with blood, and beside it stands a stūpa built at the place where a bhikṣu practicing meditation took his own life and attained the fruit of sainthood. Formerly, there was a bhikṣu who exerted his mind and body, living in seclusion to practice meditation; as the years passed, he did not attain the holy fruit. Retiring and blaming himself, he sighed privately, saying: "The fruit of the non-learner (aśaikṣa) is not attained in time; what is the use of living in this body burdened with defilements!" He then went to this rock and stabbed his own neck; at that moment, he attained the fruit of Arhatship, rose into the void, manifested spiritual transformations, transformed into fire to consume his body, and entered into extinction (parinirvāṇa). Admiring his noble conduct, they built this to record his merit. On the cliff to the east of where the bhikṣu attained the fruit, there is a stone stūpa at the place where a bhikṣu practicing meditation threw himself from the cliff and attained the fruit of sainthood. Formerly, in the time of the Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who sat in the mountain forests practicing the meditation for attaining the fruit; though he had been diligent for a long time, he could not realize the fruit, yet he continued his contemplation day and night without forgetting his tranquil meditation. The Tathāgata, knowing that his faculties were about to ripen, went there to bring it to completion; he traveled from the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana) to the foot of the mountain cliff, snapped his fingers to summon him, and stood waiting. Seeing the Holy One from afar, the bhikṣu felt great joy in body and mind and threw himself from the cliff; because of his pure heart and his respectful faith in the Buddha's words, he attained the fruit of sainthood before reaching the ground. The World-Honored One said, "You should know that now is the time." He then ascended into the void and manifested miraculous transformations. This was to make manifest his pure faith, and therefore this memorial was established.

zh: 山城北門行一里餘，至迦蘭陀竹園。今有精舍，石基甎室，東闢其戶。如來在世，多居此中，說法開化，導凡拯俗。今作如來之身。初，此城中有大長者迦蘭陀，時稱豪貴，以大竹園施諸外道。及見如來，聞法淨信，追昔竹園居彼異眾，今天人師無以館舍。時諸神鬼感其誠心，斥逐外道，而告之曰：「長者迦蘭陀當以竹園起佛精舍，汝宜速去，得免危厄。」外道憤恚，含怒而去。長者於此建立精舍，功成事畢，躬往請佛，如來是時遂受其施。
en_current: Traveling more than one *li* from the north gate of the mountain city, one arrives at the Kalandaka Bamboo Garden (迦蘭陀竹園; Skt. Veṇuvana-kalandakanivāpa). There is now a vihāra (精舍) here with a stone foundation and brick chambers, with its entrance opening to the east. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he often resided here, expounding the Dharma and transforming beings, guiding the ordinary and rescuing the worldly. Now, an image of the Tathāgata’s body has been made.  Formerly, there was a great elder in this city named Kalandaka, who was renowned for his wealth and nobility at that time. He had donated a large bamboo grove to the non-Buddhists. When he saw the Tathāgata and heard the Dharma, he developed pure faith. He reflected on how he had previously allowed the bamboo grove to be occupied by those of other sects, while the Teacher of Gods and Men now had no place to lodge. At that time, various spirits and deities, moved by his sincerity, expelled the non-Buddhists and told them, "The elder Kalandaka intends to build a Buddhist monastery in the bamboo grove; you should depart quickly to avoid danger and calamity." The non-Buddhists were resentful and departed in anger. The elder then established the monastery here; once the work was completed, he went in person to invite the Buddha, and the Tathāgata thereupon accepted his offering.

name_zh: 阿闍多設咄路王舍利塔
zh: 迦蘭陀竹園東有窣堵波，阿闍多設咄路王（唐言未生怨，舊曰阿闍世，訛略也）之所建也。如來涅槃之後，諸王共分舍利，未生怨王得以持歸，式遵崇建，而修供養。無憂王之發信心也，開取舍利，建窣堵波，尚有遺餘，時燭光景。未生怨王窣堵波，有尊者阿難半身舍利。昔尊者將寂滅也，去摩揭陀國，趣吠舍釐城。兩國交爭，欲興兵甲。尊者傷愍，遂分其身，摩揭陀王奉歸供養，即斯勝地，式修崇建。其傍則有如來經行之處。次此不遠有窣堵波，是舍利子及沒特伽羅子等安居之所。
en_current: To the east of the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove (迦蘭陀竹園) is a stūpa built by King Ajātaśatru (阿闍多設咄路王; translated in the Tang language as "Unborn Enemy" [未生怨], formerly called Ajāśatru [阿闍世], which is an erroneous abbreviation). After the Tathāgata entered nirvāṇa, the various kings divided the relics among themselves. King Ajātaśatru obtained his share and brought them back, where he formally observed the rites of construction and performed offerings. When King Aśoka (無憂王) developed faith, he opened the stūpa to retrieve the relics and built [new] stūpas; some relics still remain, and from time to time they shine with light.  In the stūpa of King Ajātaśatru, there are relics of half the body of the Venerable Ānanda. Formerly, when the Venerable One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he left the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) and headed toward the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城). The two countries were in conflict and intended to raise an army. The Venerable One felt compassion and therefore divided his body; the King of Magadha received his portion and brought it back for veneration, and at this very sacred site, he formally performed the rites of construction. Beside it is a place where the Tathāgata walked in meditation. Not far from this is a stūpa, which is the place where Śāriputra (舍利子) and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) and others resided during the rainy season.

zh: 竹林園西南行五六里，南山之陰，大竹林中，有大石室，是尊者摩訶迦葉在此與九百九十大阿羅漢，如來涅槃後結集三藏。前有故基，未生怨王為集法藏諸大羅漢建此堂宇。初，大迦葉宴坐山林，忽燭光明，又覩地震，曰：「是何祥變，若此之異？」以天眼觀，見佛世尊於雙樹林間入般涅槃，尋命徒屬趣拘尸城。路逢梵志，手執天花。迦葉問曰：「汝從何來？知我大師今在何處？」梵志對曰：「我適從彼拘尸城來，見汝大師已入涅槃，天、人大眾咸興供養，我所持花，自彼得也。」迦葉聞已，謂其徒曰：「慧日淪照，世界闇冥，善導遐棄，眾生顛墜。」懈怠比丘更相賀曰：「如來寂滅，我曹安樂，若有所犯，誰能訶制？」迦葉聞已，深更感傷，思集法藏，據教治犯。遂至雙樹，觀化禮敬。既而法王去世，人、天無導，諸大羅漢亦取滅度。時大迦葉作是思惟：「承順佛教，宜集法藏。」於是登蘇迷盧山，擊大揵稚，唱如是言：「今王舍城將有法事，諸證果人宜時速集！」揵稚聲中傳迦葉教，遍至三千大千世界，得神通者聞皆集會。是時迦葉告諸眾曰：「如來寂滅，世界空虛，當集法藏，用報佛恩。今將集法，務從簡靜，豈恃群居，不成勝業？其有具三明，得六通，聞持不謬，辯才無礙，如斯上人，可應結集。自餘果學，各歸其居。」於是得九百九十人，除阿難在學地，大迦葉召而謂曰：「汝未盡漏，宜出聖眾。」曰：「隨侍如來，多歷年所，每有法議，曾未棄遺。今將結集，而見擯斥，法王寂滅，失所依怙。」迦葉告曰：「勿懷憂惱。汝親侍佛，誠復多聞，然愛惑未盡，習結未斷。」阿難辭屈而出，至空寂處，欲取無學，勤求不證。既已疲怠，便欲假寐，未及伏枕，遂證羅漢。往結集所，叩門白至。迦葉問曰：「汝結盡耶？宜運神通，非門而入。」阿難承命，從鑰隙入，禮僧已畢，退而復坐。是時安居初十五日也。於是迦葉揚言曰：「念哉諦聽！阿難聞持，如來稱讚，集素呾纜（舊曰修多羅，訛也）藏。優波釐持律明究，眾所知識，集毘奈耶（舊曰毘那耶，訛也）藏。我迦葉波集阿毘達磨藏。」兩三月盡，集三藏訖。以大迦葉僧中上座，因而謂之上座部焉。大迦葉波結集西北，有窣堵波，是阿難受僧訶責，不預結集，至此宴坐，證羅漢果。證果之後，方乃預焉。
en_current: Traveling five or six li southwest from the Bamboo Grove (Veṇuvana), on the northern side of the South Mountain (Dakṣiṇagiri), in a great bamboo forest, there is a large stone chamber. This is where the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, together with nine hundred and ninety great arhats, compiled the Tripiṭaka after the Tathāgata’s nirvana. In front are the old foundations of a hall built by King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) for the great arhats who were to compile the Dharma-treasury.  Initially, while Mahākāśyapa was sitting in meditation in the mountain forest, he suddenly saw a brilliant light and observed the earth quake. He said, "What omen is this, that it should be so extraordinary?" Using his heavenly eye to observe, he saw that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had entered parinirvana between the twin trees, and he immediately ordered his followers to hasten to the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城). On the road, he met a Brahman holding a heavenly flower in his hand. Mahākāśyapa asked, "Where do you come from? Do you know where my Great Teacher is now?" The Brahman replied, "I have just come from that city of Kuśinagara; I saw that your Great Teacher has already entered nirvana, and the multitudes of gods and men are all making offerings. The flower I hold was obtained from there."  Upon hearing this, Mahākāśyapa said to his followers, "The sun of wisdom has set, the world is in darkness, the excellent guide has departed, and sentient beings will fall into ruin." Lax monks congratulated one another, saying, "The Tathāgata has attained extinction, so we are now at ease. If we commit any offense, who will be able to rebuke or restrain us?" Hearing this, Mahākāśyapa was deeply saddened and thought to compile the Dharma-treasury to govern offenses according to the teachings. He then went to the twin trees to view the transformation and pay his respects. Soon after, the Dharma King passed away, leaving humans and gods without a guide, and the great arhats also entered parinirvāṇa. At that time, Mahākāśyapa thought to himself, "In obedience to the Buddha’s teachings, it is appropriate to compile the Dharma-treasury." Thereupon, he ascended Mount Sumeru (蘇迷盧山), struck the great ghaṇṭā (大揵稚), and proclaimed: "A Dharma assembly is about to be held in the city of Rājagṛha (王舍城); all those who have realized the fruits of the path should assemble here with haste!" The sound of the ghaṇṭā carried the teaching of Kāśyapa, reaching throughout the trichiliomegachiliocosm, and all who possessed supernatural powers heard it and gathered.  At that time, Kāśyapa addressed the assembly, saying, "The Tathāgata has entered extinction, and the world is empty. We must compile the Dharma-treasury to repay the Buddha’s kindness. Now, in compiling the Dharma, we must prioritize simplicity and quietude; how could we rely on a large crowd and fail to accomplish this noble task? Those who possess the three knowledges (三明), have attained the six supernatural powers (六通), are endowed with perfect retention (聞持) without error, and possess unobstructed eloquence (辯才)—such superior persons may participate in the compilation. All the rest, those who hold a fruit and those still in training, should return to their respective dwellings."  Thus, he obtained nine hundred and ninety people, excluding Ānanda, who was still in the stage of learning. Mahākāśyapa summoned him and said, "You have not yet exhausted the outflows (漏); you should leave the assembly of sages." Ānanda replied, "I have attended upon the Tathāgata for many years, and whenever there were discussions on the Dharma, I was never excluded. Now that the compilation is to take place, I am being expelled; the Dharma King has entered extinction, and I have lost my refuge." Kāśyapa told him, "Do not harbor sorrow or distress. Although you have personally attended upon the Buddha and are indeed learned, your attachments and delusions have not yet been exhausted, and your habitual bonds have not yet been severed." Ānanda, silenced, withdrew and went to a quiet, secluded place, desiring to attain the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), but despite his diligent efforts, he did not attain it. Having become exhausted and weary, he intended to lie down for a moment; before his head had even touched the pillow, he attained the state of an Arhat. He went to the place of the assembly and knocked on the door to announce his arrival. Kāśyapa asked, "Have you exhausted your defilements? You should employ your supernatural powers and enter without using the door." Ānanda accepted the command, entered through the keyhole, paid homage to the monks, and then withdrew to sit down. This was on the fifteenth day, the beginning of the summer retreat.  Thereupon, Kāśyapa proclaimed aloud, "Reflect and listen carefully! Ānanda, who has heard and retained the teachings, and whom the Tathāgata praised, shall compile the Sūtra-piṭaka (素呾纜藏) (formerly called *xiuduoluo* [修多羅], which is erroneous). Upāli, who is clear and thorough in upholding the Vinaya and is recognized by the assembly, shall compile the Vinaya-piṭaka (毘奈耶藏) (formerly called *pinaye* [毘那耶], which is erroneous). I, Kāśyapa, shall compile the Abhidharma-piṭaka." After two or three months had passed, the compilation of the three piṭakas was completed. Because Mahākāśyapa was the senior elder (sthavira) among the monks, it was consequently called the Sthavira school (Sthaviravāda).  To the northwest of where Mahākāśyapa held the assembly, there is a stūpa; this is where Ānanda, having been rebuked by the monks and excluded from the assembly, came to sit in meditation and attained the fruit of Arhatship. Only after attaining this fruit was he permitted to participate.

zh: 阿難證果西行二十餘里，有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，大眾部結集之處。諸學、無學數百千人，不預大迦葉結集之眾，而來至此，更相謂曰：「如來在世，同一師學，法王寂滅，簡異我曹。欲報佛恩，當集法藏。」於是凡、聖咸會，賢智畢萃，復集素呾纜藏、毘柰耶藏、阿毘達磨藏、雜集藏、禁呪藏，別為五藏。而此結集，凡、聖同會，因而謂之大眾部。
en_current: Traveling more than twenty *li* west from the place where Ānanda attained the fruit, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the site where the Mahāsāṃghika (大眾部) held their assembly. Hundreds of thousands of learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-learners (*aśaikṣa*), not having participated in the assembly of Mahākāśyapa, came to this place and said to one another: "When the Tathāgata was in the world, we studied under the same teacher. Now that the Dharma King has passed into extinction, they have excluded us. Wishing to repay the Buddha’s kindness, we must compile the Dharma-treasury." Thereupon, the ordinary and the saintly all gathered, and the wise and the virtuous fully assembled. They compiled the Sūtra Piṭaka, the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidharma Piṭaka, the Miscellaneous Piṭaka (Saṃyukta Piṭaka), and the Dhāraṇī Piṭaka (禁呪藏), forming five separate collections. Because both ordinary people and sages assembled for this compilation, it was therefore called the Mahāsāṃghika (Great Assembly) school.

zh: 竹林精舍北行二百餘步，至迦蘭陀池，如來在昔多此說法。水既清澄，具八功德，佛涅槃後，枯涸無餘。
en_current: Going north from the Bamboo Grove Monastery (Veṇuvana-vihāra) for more than two hundred paces, one reaches the Kalandaka Pond (迦蘭陀池), where the Tathāgata often preached the Dharma in the past. Its waters were once clear and possessed the eight virtues, but after the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa, it dried up completely.

name_zh: 無憂王堵波・石柱 (迦蘭陀池西北)
zh: 迦蘭陀池西北行二三里，有窣堵波，無憂王所建也，高六十餘尺。傍有石柱，刻記立窣堵波事，高五十餘尺，上作象形。
en_current: Traveling two or three li to the northwest of the Kalandaka Pond (迦蘭陀池), there is a stupa (窣堵波) built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is over sixty feet high. Beside it is a stone pillar, inscribed with an account of the construction of the stupa, standing over fifty feet high and topped with the figure of an elephant.

name_zh: 曷羅闍姞利呬城 (王舍城)
zh: 石柱東北不遠，至曷羅闍姞利呬城（唐言王舍）。外郭已壞，無復遺堵，內城雖毀，基址猶峻，周二十餘里，面有一門。初，頻毘娑羅王都在上宮城也，編戶之家頻遭火害。一家縱逸，四隣罹災，防火不暇，資產廢業，眾庶嗟怨，不安其居。王曰：「我以不德，下民罹患，修何德可以禳之？」群臣曰：「大王德化邕穆，政教明察，今茲細民不謹，致此火災，宜制嚴科，以清後犯，若有火起，窮究先發，罰其首惡，遷之寒林。寒林者，棄屍之所，俗謂不祥之地，人絕遊往之迹。今遷於彼，同夫棄屍。既恥陋居，當自謹護。」王曰：「善，宜遍宣告居。」頃之，王宮中先自失火。謂諸臣曰：「我其遷矣。」乃命太子監攝留事，欲清國憲，故遷居焉。時吠舍釐王聞頻毘娑羅王野處寒林，整集戎旅，欲襲不虞。邊候以聞，乃建城邑。以王先舍於此，故稱王舍城也。官屬、士、庶咸徙家焉。或云：至未生怨王乃築此城，未生怨太子既嗣王位，因遂都之。逮無憂王遷都波吒釐城，以王舍城施婆羅門，故今城中無復凡民，唯婆羅門減千家耳。宮城西南隅有二小伽藍，諸國客僧往來此止，是佛昔日說法之所。次此西北有窣堵波，珠底色迦（唐言星曆。舊曰樹提伽，訛也）長者本生故里。城南門外，道左有窣堵波，如來於此說法及度羅怙羅。
en_current: Not far to the northeast of the stone pillar, one reaches the city of Rājagṛha (曷羅闍姞利呬城) (in the language of Tang, "King's Abode" [王舍]). The outer wall has already collapsed, and no remains of the ramparts are left; although the inner city is ruined, its foundations are still steep and high, measuring over twenty *li* in circumference, with one gate on each side.   Formerly, when King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) had his capital in the Upper Palace City, the households of the registered inhabitants frequently suffered from the calamity of fire. If one family was negligent, the neighbors on all four sides would suffer the disaster; the people had no time for anything but fire prevention, their properties and livelihoods were abandoned, and the masses lived in grievance and unrest. The king said, "Because of my lack of virtue, the common people suffer; what merit can I cultivate to avert this?" The ministers replied, "Your Majesty’s virtuous transformation is harmonious and peaceful, and your governance and teachings are clear and discerning. Now, these common people are not cautious, leading to these fires. It is appropriate to establish strict regulations to prevent future offenses. If a fire breaks out, investigate thoroughly to find who started it, punish the primary culprit, and banish them to the Cold Forest (寒林)."   The Cold Forest is a place where corpses are abandoned; it is commonly called an inauspicious place, and people avoid traveling there. "Now, to banish them there is the same as treating them like a corpse. Since they will be ashamed of such a lowly dwelling, they will naturally be cautious and protective." The king said, "Good; it should be announced everywhere to the residents." Shortly after, a fire broke out in the king’s own palace first. He said to his ministers, "I shall move." He then ordered the crown prince to oversee the affairs of the capital, and wishing to clarify the laws of the state, he moved his residence there. At that time, the King of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐王), hearing that King Bimbisāra was living in the open at the Cold Forest, assembled his troops with the intent to launch a surprise attack. The border guards reported this, and he then built a city. Because the king had first taken up residence here, it was called Rājagṛha (the City of the King’s Abode). The officials, the gentry, and the common people all moved their households there. Some say that it was not until King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) that this city was built; once the crown prince Ajātaśatru succeeded to the throne, he then made it his capital. By the time King Aśoka (無憂王) moved the capital to Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐城), he bestowed Rājagṛha upon the brahmans; therefore, there are no longer any common people in the city, only fewer than a thousand brahman families. In the southwest corner of the palace city are two small saṃghārāmas where visiting monks from various countries stay when they come and go; this is the place where the Buddha formerly expounded the Dharma. To the northwest of this is a stūpa, the former birthplace of the elder Jyotiṣka (珠底色迦) (in the language of Tang, "Star Calendar" [星曆]; formerly called Shutijia [樹提伽], which is erroneous). Outside the south gate of the city, to the left of the road, there is a stūpa where the Tathāgata expounded the Dharma and converted Rāhula.

zh: 中路有二小窣堵波，一謂下乘，即王至此徒行以進；一謂退凡，即簡凡人不令同往。
en_current: On the middle path there are two small stūpas: one is called "Dismounting" (Xiàchéng 下乘), marking the place where the king would arrive and proceed on foot; the other is called "Turning Back the Ordinary" (Tuìfán 退凡), marking where ordinary people were screened and not permitted to go further.

zh: 城南門外，道左有窣堵波，如來於此說法及度羅怙羅。
en_current: Outside the S gate of the city, on the left of the road, there is a stūpa; here the Tathāgata preached the Dharma and ordained Rāhula (羅怙羅).

zh: 從此北行三十餘里，至那爛陀（唐言施無厭）僧伽藍。聞之耆舊曰：此伽藍南菴沒羅林中有池，其龍名那爛陀，傍建伽藍，因取為稱。從其實議，是如來在昔修菩薩行，為大國王，建都此地，悲愍眾生，好樂周給，時美其德，號施無厭，由是伽藍因以為稱。其地本菴沒羅園，五百商人以十億金錢買以施佛，佛於此處三月說法，諸商人等亦證聖果。佛涅槃後未久，此國先王鑠迦羅阿逸多（唐言帝日），敬重一乘，遵崇三寶，式占福地，建此伽藍。初興功也，穿傷龍身，時有善占尼乾外道，見而記曰：「斯勝地也，建立伽藍，當必昌盛，為五印度之軌則，逾千載而彌隆，後進學人易以成業，然多歐血，傷龍故也。」其子佛陀毱多王（唐言覺護），繼體承統，聿遵勝業，次此之南，又建伽藍。呾他揭多毱多王（唐言如來），篤修前緒，次此之東，又建伽藍。婆羅阿迭多（唐言幼日）王之嗣位也，次此東北，又建伽藍。功成事畢，福會稱慶，輸誠幽顯，延請凡聖。其會也，五印度僧萬里雲集，眾坐已定，二僧後至，引上第三重閣。或有問曰：「王將設會，先請凡聖，大德何方，最後而至？」曰：「我至那國也，和上嬰疹，飯已方行，受王遠請，故來赴會。」問者驚駭，遽以白王。王心知聖也，躬往問焉，遲上重閣，莫知所去。王更深信，捨國出家。出家既已，位居僧末，心常怏怏，懷不自安：「我昔為王，尊居最上；今者出家，卑在眾末。」尋往白僧，自述情事。於是眾僧和合，令未受戒者以年齒為次，故此伽藍獨有斯制。其王之子代闍羅（唐言金剛），嗣位之後，信心貞固，復於此西建立伽藍。其後中印度王此北復建大伽藍。於是周垣峻峙，同為一門，既歷代君王繼世興建，窮諸剞劂，誠壯觀也。帝曰本大伽藍者，今置佛像，眾中日差四十僧就此而食，以報施主之恩。僧徒數千，並俊才高學也，德重當時，聲馳異域者，數百餘矣。戒行清白，律儀淳粹，僧有嚴制，眾咸貞素，印度諸國皆仰則焉。請益談玄，竭日不足，夙夜警誡，少長相成，其有不談三藏幽旨者，則形影自愧矣。故異域學人欲馳聲問，咸來稽疑，方流雅譽。是以竊名而遊，咸得禮重。殊方異域欲入談議，門者詰難，多屈而還；學深今古，乃得入焉。於是客遊後進，詳論藝能，其退飛者固十七八矣。二三博物，眾中次詰，莫不挫其銳、頹其名。若其高才博物，強識多能，明德哲人，聯暉繼軌。至如護法、護月，振芳塵於遺教；德慧、堅慧，流雅譽於當時；光友之清論；勝友之高談；智月則風鑒明敏；戒賢乃至德幽邃。若此上人，眾所知識，德隆先達，學貫舊章，述作論釋各十數部，並盛流通，見珍當世。伽藍四周，聖迹百數，舉其二三，可略言矣。
en_current: From here, traveling north for more than thirty *li*, one arrives at the Nālandā (translated into Chinese as "Giving Without Weariness") monastery. I heard from the elders that in the mango grove to the south of this monastery there is a pond; a dragon named Nālandā lived there, and because the monastery was built beside it, it took its name from the dragon. According to the actual account, it is because the Tathāgata, in the past when practicing the bodhisattva path, was a great king who established his capital in this place. He felt compassion for sentient beings and delighted in giving generously; at the time, people praised his virtue and called him "Giving Without Weariness," and thus the monastery took this as its name. The land was originally a mango grove; five hundred merchants bought it with ten billion gold coins and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma here for three months, and the merchants all attained the fruits of sainthood. Not long after the Buddha’s nirvana, a former king of this country named Śakrāditya (translated into Chinese as "Emperor Sun" [帝日]) deeply respected the One Vehicle and honored the Triple Gem; he selected this auspicious site by divination and built this monastery. When the work first began, they pierced and injured the body of the dragon. At that time, there was a Nirgrantha outsider skilled in divination who saw this and predicted: "This is a superior site; if a monastery is built here, it will surely flourish and become the standard for the five Indias. It will grow even more prosperous after a thousand years, and later students will easily complete their studies here. However, there will be much coughing of blood, because the dragon was injured." His son, King Buddhagupta (translated into Chinese as "Protector of Awakening"), succeeded to the throne and, following the noble legacy, built another monastery to the south of this one. King Tathāgatagupta (translated into Chinese as "Thus-Come") earnestly followed the noble legacy and built another monastery to the east of this one. When King Bālāditya (translated into Chinese as "Young Sun") succeeded to the throne, he built another monastery to the northeast of this one. When the work was completed and the ceremonies finished, he held a celebratory feast of merit, expressing his sincerity to both the hidden and the manifest, and invited both the ordinary and the holy. At this assembly, monks from the five Indias gathered from ten thousand miles away. Once the assembly was seated, two monks arrived late and were led up to the third-story pavilion. Someone asked, "The King is holding this assembly and has invited the ordinary and the holy; from what place do you venerable ones come, that you arrive last?" They replied, "We have come from the country of Cīna (至那國); our teacher was suffering from an illness, so we departed only after he had eaten. Having received the King’s distant invitation, we have come to attend the assembly." The questioner was astonished and immediately reported this to the King. The King, knowing in his heart that they were sages, went in person to inquire of them, but when he arrived at the upper pavilion, he did not know where they had gone. The King’s faith deepened further, and he renounced his kingdom to become a monk. Once he had become a monk, he was ranked at the very end of the assembly, which left him constantly dissatisfied and uneasy, thinking: "I was once a king, occupying the highest and most honorable position; now that I have become a monk, I am ranked at the very end of the assembly." He soon went to inform the monks and recounted his situation. Thereupon, the assembly of monks reached a consensus, decreeing that those who have not yet received the full precepts shall be ranked according to their age; thus, this monastery alone possesses this rule. The King’s son, Vajra (translated into Chinese as "Diamond"), possessed a firm and steadfast faith; after succeeding to the throne, he built another monastery to the west of this site. Afterward, the King of Central India built another great monastery to the north of this one. Thereupon, the surrounding walls were raised high, and they were joined into a single gate; since successive kings have built them generation after generation, exhausting all the arts of carving and joinery, it is truly a magnificent sight. In the original great monastery of Śakrāditya (帝日), a Buddha image is now installed, and forty monks are dispatched from the assembly daily to eat here in order to repay the kindness of the donors. The number of monks is several thousand, all of whom are men of outstanding talent and high learning; those whose virtue is esteemed in the present age and whose fame has spread to foreign lands number more than several hundred. Their conduct in the precepts is pure and white, and their monastic discipline is refined and perfect; the monks have strict regulations, and the assembly is entirely upright and simple, such that all the countries of India look to them as a model. They seek instruction and discuss profound mysteries, finding the whole day insufficient; they remain vigilant and admonish one another day and night, with the old and young helping each other to perfection, and if there were any who did not discuss the subtle meanings of the Tripitaka, they would feel ashamed of their own shadows. Therefore, scholars from foreign lands who wish to spread their reputation all come here to resolve their doubts, and only then does their elegant fame flow forth. For this reason, even those who travel about falsely claiming its name are everywhere treated with respect. When those from distant regions and foreign lands wish to enter for discussion, the gatekeepers pose difficult questions, and many are forced to turn back; only those who are deeply learned in both ancient and modern studies are permitted to enter. Consequently, when visiting scholars and newcomers discuss their arts and abilities in detail, those who are forced to retreat are certainly seven or eight out of every ten. As for the few who are broadly learned, they are questioned in turn by the assembly, and there is none whose sharpness is not blunted and whose reputation is not diminished. As for those of eminent talent and broad learning, possessing strong memories and many abilities, these virtuous and wise men join their brilliance and follow in the footsteps of their predecessors. As for Dharmapāla (護法) and Candrapāla (護月), they stirred the fragrant dust of the Buddha’s legacy; Guṇamati (德慧) and Sthiramati (堅慧) spread their elegant reputations throughout their time; there were the refined discourses of Prabhāmitra (光友) and the lofty discussions of Jinamitra (勝友); Candrakīrti (智月) was clear and keen in his discernment; and Śīlabhadra (戒賢) possessed virtue that was sublime and profound. These superior men were known to all; their virtue excelled that of their predecessors, and their learning encompassed the ancient texts; each composed more than ten treatises and commentaries, which were widely circulated and highly valued by their contemporaries. Around the monastery, there are hundreds of sacred traces; I shall cite two or three of them as a brief summary.

name_zh: 精舍 (如來三月說法處, 那爛陀伽藍西)
zh: 伽藍西不遠有精舍，在昔如來三月止此，為諸天、人廣說妙法。南百餘步小窣堵波，遠方比丘見佛處。昔有比丘自遠方來，至此遇見如來聖眾，內發敬心，五體投地，便即發願求輪王位。如來見已，告諸眾曰：「彼比丘者甚可愍惜。福德深遠，信心堅固，若求佛果，不久當證。今其發願求轉輪王，於當來世必受此報。身體投地下至金輪，其中所有微塵之數，一一塵是一輪王報也。既耽世樂，聖果斯遠。」其南則有觀自在菩薩立像。或見執香爐往佛精舍，周旋右繞。觀自在菩薩像南窣堵波中，有如來三月之間剃剪髮、爪。有嬰疾病，旋繞多愈。其西垣外池側窣堵波，是外道執雀於此問佛死生之事。次東南垣內五十餘步，有奇樹，高八九尺，其幹兩披，在昔如來嚼楊枝棄地，因植根柢，歲月雖久，初無增減。次東大精舍，高二百餘尺，如來在昔於此四月說諸妙法。次北百餘步精舍中，有觀自在菩薩像，淨信之徒興供養者所見不同，莫定其所，或立門側，或出簷前，諸國法俗咸來供養。觀自在菩薩精舍北有大精舍，高三百餘尺，婆羅阿迭多王之所建也，莊嚴度量及中佛像，同菩提樹下大精舍。其東北窣堵波，在昔如來於此七日演說妙法。西北則有過去四佛坐處。其南鍮石精舍，戒日王之所建立，功雖未畢，然其圖量十丈而後成之。次東二百餘步垣外，有銅立佛像，高八十餘尺，重閣六層，乃得彌覆，昔滿胄王之所作也。滿胄王銅佛像北二三里，甎精舍中，有多羅菩薩像。其量既高，其靈甚察。每歲元日，盛興供養，隣境國王、大臣、豪族，齎妙香花，持寶旛蓋，金石遞奏，絲竹相和，七日之中，建斯法會。其垣南門內有大井。昔在佛世，有大商侶，熱渴逼迫，來至佛所。世尊指其地，以可得水。商主乃以車軸築地，地既為陷，水遂泉涌。飲已聞法，皆悟聖果。
en_current: Not far to the west of the monastery (saṃghārāma) is a vihāra (精舍). In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for three months, extensively expounding the wonderful Dharma for the devas and humans. More than one hundred paces to the south is a small stupa, the place where a bhikṣu from a distant land saw the Buddha. Long ago, a bhikṣu came from a distant land and, upon arriving here, encountered the Tathāgata and his holy assembly. Internally giving rise to a heart of reverence, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and immediately made a vow to seek the position of a wheel-turning king (cakravartin). Having seen this, the Tathāgata told the assembly: "That bhikṣu is truly to be pitied. His merit and virtue are deep and far-reaching, and his faith is firm; if he were to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, he would soon attain it. Now, however, he has made a vow to seek the position of a wheel-turning king, and in a future life, he will certainly receive this reward. From the place where his body touched the ground down to the golden wheel, the number of all the minute dust particles contained therein—each and every dust particle represents the reward of a wheel-turning king. Since he indulges in worldly pleasures, the holy fruit is far off." To the south of this is a standing statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Sometimes he is seen holding an incense burner, going toward the Buddha’s vihāra, and circling it to the right. In the stupa to the south of the statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara are the hair and fingernails of the Tathāgata, shorn and clipped during those three months. Those who are afflicted with illness often recover by circumambulating it. The stupa by the side of the pond outside the western wall is where a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), holding a bird, questioned the Buddha about the matter of life and death. More than fifty paces to the southeast, within the enclosure, is a marvelous tree eight or nine feet high with its trunk divided into two; in the past, the Tathāgata chewed a willow twig and threw it on the ground, where it took root, and although a long time has passed, it has neither increased nor decreased. To the east is a great vihara, over two hundred feet high, where the Tathāgata in the past expounded the wonderful Dharma for four months. To the north, one hundred and some paces away, is a vihara containing an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩). Those of pure faith who come to make offerings see it differently, and its position cannot be fixed; sometimes it stands by the side of the door, and sometimes it appears before the eaves. The clergy and laity of various countries all come to make offerings. To the north of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva vihara is a great vihara, over three hundred feet high, built by King Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多王); its ornamentation, dimensions, and the Buddha image within are the same as those of the great vihara under the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree. To its northeast is a stūpa where the Tathāgata in the past expounded the wonderful Dharma for seven days. To the northwest is the place where the four past Buddhas sat. To its south is a brass vihara built by King Śīlāditya (戒日王); although the work is not yet finished, according to its plans and measurements, it will be one hundred feet high when completed. To the east, two hundred and some paces outside the enclosure, is a standing copper Buddha image, over eighty feet high, which required a six-story pavilion to cover it; it was made in the past by King Pūrṇavarman (滿胄王). Two or three li north of the copper Buddha image of King Pūrṇavarman, inside a brick vihara, is an image of the Bodhisattva Tārā (多羅菩薩). Its stature is lofty, and its spiritual efficacy is very manifest. Every year on the first day of the year, grand offerings are made; kings of neighboring regions, ministers, and noble families bring wonderful incense and flowers, hold precious banners and canopies, play metal and stone instruments in succession, and harmonize them with string and bamboo instruments, holding this Dharma assembly for seven days. Inside the south gate of the enclosure, there is a large well. Formerly, in the time of the Buddha, a large company of merchants, pressed by heat and thirst, came to where the Buddha was. The World-Honored One pointed to the ground, indicating that water could be obtained there. The leader of the merchants then struck the ground with a cart axle; once the ground was indented, water gushed forth like a spring. Having drunk and heard the Dharma, they all realized the holy fruit.

zh: 伽藍西南行八九里，至拘理迦邑，中有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，是尊者沒特伽羅子本生故里。傍有窣堵波，尊者於此入無餘涅槃，其中則有遺身舍利。尊者，大婆羅門種，與舍利子少為親友。舍利子以才明見貴，尊者以精鑒延譽，才智相比，動止必俱，結要終始，契同去就，相與厭俗，共求捨家，遂師珊闍耶焉。舍利子遇馬勝阿羅漢，聞法悟聖，還為尊者重述，聞而悟法，遂證初果。與其徒二百五十人俱到佛所，世尊遙見，指告眾曰：「彼來者，我弟子中神足第一。」既至佛所，請入法中。世尊告曰：「善來，比丘，淨修梵行，得離苦際。」聞是語時，鬚髮落，俗裳變，戒品淨，威儀調順。經七日，結漏盡，證羅漢果，得神通力。沒特伽羅子故里東行三四里，有窣堵波，頻毘娑羅王迎見佛處。如來初證佛果，知摩揭陀國人心渴仰，受頻毘娑羅王請，於晨朝時，著衣持鉢，與千比丘左右圍繞，皆是耆舊螺髻梵志，慕法染衣，前後羽從，入王舍城。時帝釋天王變為摩那婆，首冠螺髻，左手執金瓶，右手持寶杖，足蹈空虛，離地四指，在大眾中前導佛路。時摩揭陀國頻毘娑羅王與其國內諸婆羅門、長者、居士，百千萬眾，前後導從，出王舍城奉迎聖眾。
en_current: Traveling eight or nine li southwest from the monastery, one reaches the town of Kolika (拘理迦邑), where there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; this is the native village of the Venerable Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子). Beside it is a stūpa marking the place where the Venerable One entered the nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa), and it contains his bodily relics. The Venerable One was of a great Brahmin lineage and had been a close friend of Śāriputra since youth. Śāriputra was esteemed for his brilliant talent, while the Venerable One was renowned for his profound discernment; they were equals in wisdom, always together in their movements, bound by a lifelong pact to share the same path, and together they grew weary of the secular world and sought to leave the householder's life, eventually taking Sañjaya as their teacher. Śāriputra encountered the arhat Aśvajit, heard the Dharma, and attained realization; he returned and recounted it to the Venerable One, who, upon hearing and realizing the Dharma, attained the first fruit. Together with his two hundred and fifty disciples, he went to the place of the Buddha. The World-Honored One saw them from afar and, pointing them out to the assembly, said: "Those who are coming are the foremost in supernatural powers among my disciples." Upon arriving at the place of the Buddha, they requested to enter the Dharma. The World-Honored One said: "Welcome, monks; practice the holy life purely to reach the end of suffering." Upon hearing these words, their hair and beards fell away, their secular garments changed, their precepts became pure, and their deportment became harmonious. After seven days, their defilements were exhausted, they attained the fruit of arhatship, and they gained supernatural powers. Three or four li to the east of the native village of Maudgalyāyana, there is a stūpa at the place where King Bimbisāra went to meet and see the Buddha. When the Tathāgata first realized the fruit of buddhahood, he knew that the hearts of the people in the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) were thirsting with longing. He accepted the invitation of King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) and, in the early morning, donned his robes and took up his alms bowl. Surrounded on all sides by a thousand bhikṣus—all of whom were elder brahmans with shell-shaped topknots who had donned dyed robes out of admiration for the Dharma, following him in his retinue—he entered the city of Rājagṛha (王舍城). At that time, the heavenly king Śakra (帝釋天王) transformed himself into a māṇava (摩那婆) with a shell-shaped topknot on his head. Holding a golden vase in his left hand and a precious staff in his right, his feet treading on empty space four finger-widths above the ground, he led the way for the Buddha amidst the assembly. Then King Bimbisāra of the country of Magadha, together with the various brahmans, elders, and laypeople of his kingdom—a multitude of hundreds of thousands—came out of the city of Rājagṛha in a procession to welcome the holy assembly.

zh: 頻毘娑羅王迎佛東南行二十餘里，至迦羅臂拏迦邑，中有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。是尊者舍利子本生故里，井今尚在。傍有窣堵波，尊者於此寂滅，其中則有遺身舍利。尊者，大婆羅門種。其父高才博識，深鑒精微，凡諸典籍莫不究習。其妻感夢，具告夫曰：「吾昨宵寐，夢感異人，身被鎧甲，手執金剛，摧破諸山，退立一山之下。」夫曰：「夢甚善。汝當生男，達學貫世，摧諸論師，破其宗致，唯不如一人，為作弟子。」果而有娠，母忽聰明，高論劇談，言無屈滯。尊者年始八歲，名擅四方，其性淳質，其心慈悲，朽壞結縛，成就智慧。與沒特伽羅子少而相友，深厭塵俗，未有所歸，於是與沒特伽羅子於珊闍耶外道所而修習焉。乃相謂曰：「斯非究竟之理，未能窮苦際也。各求明導，先嘗甘露，必同其味。」時大阿羅漢馬勝執持應器，入城乞食。舍利子見其威儀閑雅，即而問曰：「汝師是誰？」曰：「釋種太子厭世出家，成等正覺。是我師也。」舍利子曰：「所說何法，可得聞乎？」曰：「我初受教，未達深義。」舍利子曰：「願說所聞。」馬勝乃隨宜演說，舍利子聞已，即證初果。遂與其徒二百五十人往詣佛所，世尊遙見，指告眾曰：「我弟子中智慧第一。」至已頂禮，願從佛法。世尊告曰：「善來，比丘。」聞是語時，戒品具足。過半月後，聞佛為長爪梵志說法，聞餘論而感悟，遂證羅漢之果。其後阿難承佛告寂滅期，展轉相語，各懷悲感，舍利子深增戀仰，不忍見佛入般涅槃，遂請世尊，先入寂滅。世尊告曰：「宜知是時。」告謝門人，至本生里，侍者沙彌遍告城邑。未生怨王及其國人莫不風馳，皆悉雲會。舍利子廣為說法，聞已而去。於後夜分，正意繫心，入滅盡定，從定起已而寂滅焉。迦羅臂挐迦邑東南四五里，有窣堵波，是尊者舍利子門人入涅槃處。或曰：迦葉波佛在世時，有三拘胝（拘胝者，唐言億）大阿羅漢同於此地無餘寂滅。
en_current: From the place where King Bimbisāra welcomed the Buddha, traveling more than twenty *li* to the southeast, one arrives at the town of Kālapināka (迦羅臂拏迦邑). In it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. This is the native village of the Venerable Śāriputra, and the well still exists today. Beside it is a stūpa where the Venerable entered into extinction, which contains his bodily relics. The Venerable was of a great Brahmin lineage. His father was highly talented and broadly learned, with a deep insight into the subtle and profound; there was no classic or treatise that he had not thoroughly studied. His wife had a dream and told her husband in detail, saying: "Last night in my sleep, I dreamt of a strange man clad in armor and holding a vajra, who demolished all the mountains and then stood back beneath a single mountain." Her husband said: "This is a very auspicious dream. You will give birth to a son who will be learned and peerless in the world, who will defeat all the masters of debate and shatter their doctrines, but who will be inferior to only one person, to whom he will become a disciple." She was indeed pregnant, and the mother suddenly became brilliant, engaging in high-level discussions and intense debates with speech that was never obstructed. When the Venerable was eight years old, his fame spread to the four quarters; his nature was pure and simple, his heart was compassionate, he destroyed the bonds of defilement, and he attained wisdom. He and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) had been friends since youth and were deeply weary of the dusty world, yet they had not found a place to turn. Thereupon, he and Maudgalyāyana went to the place of the non-Buddhist Sañjaya (珊闍耶) to study. They then said to each other: "This is not the ultimate principle, and it cannot exhaust the limits of suffering. Let us each seek a clear guide; whoever tastes the nectar first must share its flavor with the other." At that time, the great arhat Aśvajit (馬勝) held his alms bowl and entered the city to beg for food. Śāriputra (舍利子) saw his dignified and refined demeanor and immediately asked him, "Who is your teacher?" He replied, "The prince of the Śākya clan, who grew weary of the world, renounced household life, and attained equal and perfect enlightenment—he is my teacher." Śāriputra said, "What dharma does he teach? May I hear it?" He replied, "I have only recently received instruction and have not yet grasped the profound meaning." Śāriputra said, "I wish to hear what you have heard." Aśvajit then expounded it according to the occasion, and upon hearing it, Śāriputra immediately attained the first fruit. He then went with his two hundred and fifty disciples to the place of the Buddha. The World-Honored One saw them from afar and, pointing them out, told the assembly, "Among my disciples, he is the foremost in wisdom." Upon arriving, he bowed his head to the ground and wished to follow the Buddha’s dharma. The World-Honored One said, "Welcome, bhikṣu." Upon hearing these words, his precepts were fully perfected. More than half a month later, he heard the Buddha preaching to the Long-nailed Brahmacārin (長爪梵志), and upon hearing the remaining discourse, he was enlightened and attained the fruit of an arhat. Later, when Ānanda (阿難) received the Buddha’s announcement of the time of his extinction, the news was passed from one to another, and all were filled with sorrow and grief. Śāriputra’s longing and reverence deepened, and, unable to bear seeing the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa, he requested the World-Honored One to let him enter extinction first. The World-Honored One said, "You should know the time." He took leave of his disciples and went to his native village, where his attendant novice informed the entire city. King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) and the people of his country all rushed there like the wind, gathering like clouds. Śāriputra (舍利子) preached the Dharma extensively, and having heard him, the people departed. During the last watch of the night, he focused his mind and entered the samādhi of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); upon arising from that meditation, he entered final extinction. Four or five li to the southeast of the town of Kālapināka (迦羅臂挐迦邑), there is a stūpa at the place where the disciples of the Venerable Śāriputra entered nirvāṇa. Some say that when Kāśyapa Buddha (迦葉波佛) was in the world, three koṭis (*koṭi* is, in the language of Tang, *yi* [億]) of great arhats entered nirvāṇa without remainder at this same place.

zh: 舍利子門人窣堵波東行三十餘里，至因陀羅勢羅窶訶山（唐言帝釋窟）。其山巖谷杳冥，花林蓊欝，嶺有兩峯，岌然特起。西峯南巖間有大石室，廣而不高，昔如來嘗於中止。時時天帝釋以四十二疑事畫石請問，佛為演釋，其迹猶在。今作此像，擬昔聖儀，入中禮敬者，莫不肅然驚懼。山巖上有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。東峯上有伽藍，聞諸土俗曰：其中僧眾，或於夜分，望見西峯石室佛像前每有燈炬，常為照燭。因陀羅勢羅窶訶山東峯伽藍前有窣堵波，謂亘（許贈反）娑（唐言雁）。昔此伽藍習翫小乘，小乘漸教也，故開三淨之食，而此伽藍遵而不墜。其後三淨求不時獲。有比丘經行，忽見群雁飛翔，戲言曰：「今日眾僧中食不充，摩訶薩埵宜知是時。」言聲未絕，一雁退飛，當其僧前，投身自殞。比丘見已，具白眾僧，聞者悲感，咸相謂曰：「如來設法，導誘隨機；我等守愚，遵行漸教。大乘者，正理也，宜改先執，務從聖旨。此雁垂誡，誠為明導，宜旌厚德，傳記終古。」於是建窣堵波，式昭遺烈，以彼死雁瘞其下焉。
en_current: Going thirty-some *li* to the east of the stupa of the disciples of Śāriputra, one arrives at the mountain of Indraśailaguhā (Indra-śaila-guhā; in the language of Tang, "Cave of Śakra"). The mountain’s rocky valleys are deep and dark, and its flowering forests are lush and dense; on the ridge are two peaks that rise prominently and steeply. Between the southern cliffs of the western peak is a large stone chamber, wide but not high, where the Tathāgata once stayed. From time to time, the Heavenly Lord Śakra would carve forty-two questions of doubt onto the stone to ask [the Buddha], and the Buddha would explain them; those traces still remain. Today, an image has been made there to emulate the sacred appearance of the past, and those who enter to pay homage are all filled with awe and trepidation. On the mountain cliffs are the sites of the sitting and walking meditation traces of the four past Buddhas. On the eastern peak is a monastery; I heard from the local people that the monks there sometimes see, during the night, lamps and torches shining as constant illumination before the Buddha image in the stone chamber of the western peak. In front of the monastery on the eastern peak of Indraśailaguhā Mountain is a stupa called Haṃsa (亘娑) (亘 is pronounced x[u] + [z]eng) (in the language of Tang, "Goose"). Formerly, this monastery practiced the Lesser Vehicle; the Lesser Vehicle is a gradual teaching, and therefore permitted the consumption of the three pure meats, a practice this monastery followed and did not abandon. Later, the three pure meats were not always obtainable. A monk who was walking in meditation suddenly saw a flock of geese flying by and jokingly said, "Today the midday meal for the monks is insufficient; the Mahāsattvas should know the time." Before his words had ceased, one goose flew back, landed before the monk, and cast its body down to die. After the bhikṣu saw this, he reported it fully to the assembly of monks.
