The master of treatises (śāstra-master) stepped across the threshold and announced to the crowd, "I have long prayed, waiting to see Maitreya (慈氏); through the protection of the holy spirits, my great vow is now fulfilled. You should all enter here to witness the arising of the Buddha together." Those who heard this were terrified and none dared to step through the entrance, claiming it was a den of venomous snakes and fearing they would lose their lives. After he exhorted them repeatedly, only six people followed him inside. The master of treatises looked back to bid farewell to the crowd and entered with composure. Once he had entered, the stone wall closed back up. The crowd all lamented and sighed, regretting their previous words.

zh: 自此西南行千餘里，至珠利耶國（南印度境）。珠利耶國，周二千四五百里。國大都城周十餘里。土野空曠，藪澤荒蕪。居戶寡少，群盜公行。氣序溫暑，風俗姦宄。人性獷烈，崇信外道。伽藍頹毀，粗有僧徒。天祠數十所，多露形外道也。城東南不遠有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。如來在昔曾於此處現大神通，說深妙法，摧伏外道，度諸天人。城西不遠有故伽藍，提婆菩薩與羅漢論議之處。初，提婆菩薩聞此伽藍有嗢呾羅（唐言上）阿羅漢，得六神通，具八解脫，遂來遠尋，觀其風範。既至伽藍，投羅漢宿。羅漢少欲知足，唯置一床。提婆既至，無以為席，乃聚落葉，指令就坐。羅漢入定，夜分方出。提婆於是陳疑請決，羅漢隨難為釋，提婆尋聲重質，第七轉已，杜口不酬，竊運神通力，往覩史多天請問慈氏。慈氏為釋，因而告曰：「彼提婆者，曠劫修行，賢劫之中，當紹佛位，非爾所知，宜深禮敬。」如彈指頃，還復本座，乃復抑揚妙義，剖析微言。提婆謂曰：「此慈氏菩薩聖智之釋也，豈仁者所能詳究哉？」羅漢曰：「然，如來旨。」於是避席禮謝，深加敬歎。
en_current: From here, traveling southwest for more than a thousand *li*, one reaches the country of Cuḷya (珠利耶國) (in the region of South India). The country of Cuḷya is two thousand four or five hundred *li* in circumference. The capital city is more than ten *li* in circumference. The land is wild and desolate, with marshes and wastes. The population is sparse, and bands of robbers operate openly. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are treacherous. The people are fierce and violent by nature, and they revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths. The monasteries are dilapidated, with only a few monks. There are several dozen *deva* temples, mostly belonging to the naked ascetics. Not far to the southeast of the city is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata manifested great supernatural powers at this place, preached the profound and subtle Dharma, subdued the non-Buddhists, and saved various heavenly beings and humans. Not far to the west of the city is an old monastery, the place where the Bodhisattva Deva debated with an Arhat. Initially, the Bodhisattva Deva heard that there was an Arhat in this monastery named Uttara (*Uttara* is translated as "Superior" in Chinese), who had attained the six supernatural powers and was endowed with the eight emancipations; he therefore came from afar to seek him out and observe his demeanor. Upon arriving at the monastery, he requested to stay with the Arhat. The Arhat was of few desires and knew contentment, possessing only one bed. When Deva arrived, there was nothing to use as a seat, so he gathered fallen leaves and instructed him to sit upon them. The Arhat entered into meditation and did not emerge until midnight. Deva then presented his doubts and requested resolutions; the Arhat explained each difficulty as it was raised. Deva followed his words with repeated questioning, and by the seventh round, the Arhat remained silent and could not respond, so he secretly exercised his supernatural powers to go to the Tuṣita Heaven to consult Maitreya. Maitreya (慈氏) provided the explanation and told him: "That Deva (提婆) has practiced for vast kalpas and shall succeed to the Buddha's throne during the Bhadrakalpa (賢劫); this is beyond your knowledge, and you should pay him deep respect." In the space of a finger-snap, he returned to his original seat, whereupon he expounded the wonderful meanings and analyzed the subtle words. Deva said to him: "This is the explanation from the holy wisdom of Maitreya Bodhisattva; how could it be something you have investigated thoroughly on your own?" The Arhat replied: "Indeed, it is the intent of the Tathāgata." Thereupon, he left his seat to offer thanks and expressed deep reverence and admiration.

zh: 從此南入林野中，行千五六百里，至達羅毘荼國（南印度境）。達羅毘荼國，周六千餘里，國大都城號逮志補羅，周三十餘里。土地沃壤，稼穡豐盛，多花菓，出寶物。氣序溫暑，風俗勇烈。深篤信義，高尚博識，而語言、文字少異中印度。伽藍百餘所，僧徒萬餘人，皆遵學上座部法。天祠八十餘所，多露形外道也。如來在世，數遊此國，說法度人，故無憂王於諸聖迹皆建窣堵波。逮志補羅城者，即達磨波羅（唐言護法）菩薩本生之城。菩薩，此國大臣之長子也。幼懷雅量，長而弘遠。年方弱冠，王姬下降。禮筵之夕，憂心慘悽，對佛像前殷懃祈請。至誠所感，神負遠遁，去此數百里，至山伽藍，坐佛堂中。有僧開戶，見此少年，疑其盜也，更詰問之，菩薩具懷指告，因請出家。眾咸驚異，遂允其志。王乃宣命，推求遐邇，乃知菩薩神負遠塵。王之知也，增深敬異。自染衣已，篤學精勤，令問風範，語在前記。城南不遠有大伽藍，國中聰叡同類萃止。有窣堵波，高百餘尺，無憂王所建也。如來在昔於此說法，摧伏外道，廣度人、天。其側則有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。
en_current: From here, traveling south into the wilderness for fifteen or sixteen hundred li, one reaches the country of Draviḍa (達羅毘荼國) (in the territory of South India). The country of Draviḍa is over six thousand li in circumference, and its capital city, called Kāñcīpura (逮志補羅), is over thirty li in circumference. The land is fertile and rich, with abundant crops, many flowers and fruits, and it produces precious treasures. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are brave and fierce. They are deeply devoted to faith and righteousness, and are noble and learned, though their language and script differ slightly from those of Central India. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas and more than ten thousand monks, all of whom follow the teachings of the Sthavira school. There are over eighty Deva temples, mostly belonging to the naked ascetics. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled to this country to preach the Dharma and save people, and for this reason, King Aśoka (無憂王) built stūpas at all the sacred sites. The city of Kāñcīpura is the birthplace of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (達磨波羅) (in Tang language, "Protector of the Dharma"). The Bodhisattva was the eldest son of a high minister of this country. In his youth, he possessed a refined character, and as he grew, his aspirations became vast. When he reached the age of twenty, a princess was betrothed to him. On the evening of the wedding ceremony, he felt deeply distressed and prayed earnestly before an image of the Buddha. Moved by his utmost sincerity, a deity carried him far away to a mountain saṃghārāma several hundred li from there, where he sat within the Buddha hall. A monk opened the door and, seeing this youth, suspected him of being a thief and questioned him further. The Bodhisattva explained his situation in full and requested to leave the household life. The assembly was astonished and subsequently granted his wish. The king then issued a decree to search far and near, and thus learned that the Bodhisattva had been carried away to a distant land by a deity. Upon learning this, the king’s respect and wonder increased all the more. After the Bodhisattva had dyed his robes (i.e., entered the monastic life), he studied with diligent sincerity, and his excellent reputation and conduct are described in the preceding record. Not far to the south of the city is a large saṃghārāma where the wise and learned of the country gather and reside. There is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, subduing the followers of external paths and extensively saving humans and devas. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

zh: 自此南行三千餘里，至秣羅矩吒國（亦謂枳秣羅國。南印度境）。秣羅矩吒國，周五千餘里。國大都城周四十餘里。土田舃鹵，地利不滋。海渚諸珍，多聚此國。氣序炎熱，人多釐黑。志性剛烈，邪正兼崇。不尚遊藝，唯善逐利。伽藍故基，寔多餘址，存者既少，僧徒亦寡。天祠數百，外道甚眾，多露形之徒也。城東不遠有故伽藍，庭宇荒蕪，基址尚在，無憂王弟大帝之所建也。其東有窣堵波，崇基已陷，覆鉢猶存，無憂王之所建立。在昔如來於此說法，現大神通，度無量眾，用彰聖迹，故此標建。歲久彌神，祈願或遂。
en_current: From here, traveling south for more than three thousand *li*, one reaches the country of Malakūṭa (秣羅矩吒國) (also called the country of Kumārī (枳秣羅國); it is within the borders of South India). The country of Malakūṭa is more than five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is more than forty *li* in circuit. The soil is salty and barren, and the land is not fertile. Many precious items from the islands of the sea are gathered in this country. The climate is hot, and the people are mostly dark-skinned. Their dispositions are fierce and unyielding, and they revere both heterodox and orthodox teachings. They do not value the arts, but are skilled only in the pursuit of profit. There are many ruins of old monasteries, but few remain standing, and the monks are also scarce. There are several hundred *deva* temples, and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are very numerous, many of whom are ascetics who go naked. Not far to the east of the city is an old monastery; its courtyards and buildings are desolate, but the foundations still remain, having been built by the Great King (Mahendra), the younger brother of King Aśoka. To its east is a *stūpa* whose high foundation has sunk, though the inverted-bowl dome still exists, established by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, manifested great supernatural powers, and saved immeasurable multitudes; this was built to mark these sacred traces. As time has passed, it has become increasingly miraculous, and prayers are sometimes fulfilled.

zh: 國南濱海有秣剌耶山，崇崖峻嶺，洞谷深㵎。其中則有白檀香樹、栴檀儞婆樹。樹類白檀，不可以別，唯於盛夏，登高遠瞻，其有大蛇縈者，於是知之。猶其木性涼冷，故蛇盤也。既望見已，射箭為記，冬蟄之後，方乃採伐。羯布羅香樹松身異葉，花菓斯別，初採既濕，尚未有香，木乾之後，循理而析，其中有香，狀若雲母，色如氷雪，此所謂龍腦香也。
en_current: To the south of the country, bordering the sea, is Mount Malaya (秣剌耶山), with its lofty cliffs, steep ridges, deep caverns, and mountain torrents. Among them are white sandalwood trees and candaneva trees (栴檀儞婆樹). The latter resemble white sandalwood and cannot be distinguished from them, except in the height of summer, when one climbs to a high place and looks out from afar; those entwined by large snakes are known to be such. Because the nature of this wood is cool and cold, the snakes coil around it. Once they have been sighted, arrows are shot to mark them, and only after the snakes have hibernated in winter are the trees harvested. The camphor tree (羯布羅香樹; Skt. karpūra) has a trunk like a pine but different leaves, and its flowers and fruits are also distinct. When first harvested and still moist, it has no fragrance, but after the wood dries, it is split along the grain to reveal a fragrant substance within, shaped like mica and colored like ice or snow; this is what is called camphor (龍腦香).

zh: 秣剌耶山東有布呾洛迦山，山徑危險，巖谷敧傾，山頂有池，其水澄鏡，流出大河，周流繞山二十匝，入南海。池側有石天宮，觀自在菩薩往來遊舍。其有願見菩薩者，不顧身命，厲水登山，忘其艱險，能達之者，蓋亦寡矣。而山下居人，祈心請見，或作自在天形，或為塗灰外道，慰喻其人，果遂其願。
en_current: To the east of the Malaya (秣剌耶) Mountains is Mount Potalaka (布呾洛迦山). The mountain paths are perilous, and the cliffs and valleys are precipitous. On the summit of the mountain is a lake with water as clear as a mirror, from which flows a great river that circles the mountain twenty times before entering the South Sea. Beside the lake is a stone celestial palace where the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) comes and goes to dwell. Those who wish to see the Bodhisattva disregard their own lives, wading through waters and climbing the mountain, forgetting all hardships and dangers; yet those who are able to reach it are few indeed. As for the inhabitants at the foot of the mountain who pray with a sincere heart to see him, the Bodhisattva may appear in the form of Maheśvara (自在天) or as an ash-smearing ascetic (塗灰外道) to console them and fulfill their wishes.

zh: 從此山東北海畔有城，是往南海僧伽羅國路。聞諸土俗曰：從此入海，東南可三千餘里，至僧伽羅國（唐言執師子，非印度之境）。
en_current: To the northeast of this mountain, by the seaside, there is a city which is on the route to the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) in the South Sea. I have heard from the local people that if one enters the sea from here and travels southeast for more than three thousand li, one reaches the country of Siṃhala (in the language of the Tang, this means "Holder of Lions"; it is not within the borders of India).

zh: 僧伽羅國，周七千餘里。國大都城周四十餘里。土地沃壤，氣序溫暑，稼穡時播，花果具繁。人戶殷盛，家產富饒。其形卑黑，其性獷烈。好學尚德，崇善勤福。此國本寶渚也，多有珍寶，棲止鬼神。其後南印度有一國王，女娉隣國，吉日送歸，路逢師子，侍衛之徒棄女逃難，女居輿中，心甘喪命。時師子王負女而去，入深山，處幽谷，捕鹿採菓，以時資給，既積歲月，遂孕男女，形貌同人，性種畜也。男漸長大，力格猛獸。年方弱冠，人智斯發，謂其母曰：「我何謂乎？父則野獸，母乃是人，既非族類，如何配偶？」母乃述昔事以告其子，曰：「人畜殊途，宜速逃逝。」母曰：「我先已逃，不能自濟。」其子於後逐師子父，登山踰嶺，察其遊止，可以逃難。伺父去已，遂擔負母妹，下趨人里。母曰：「宜各慎密，勿說事源，人或知聞，輕鄙我等。」於是至父本國，國非家族，宗祀已滅。投寄邑人，人謂之曰：「爾曹何國人也？」曰：「我本此國，流離異域，子母相携，來歸故里。」人皆哀愍，更共資給。其師子王還無所見，追戀男女，憤恚既發，便出山谷，往來村邑，咆哮震吼，暴害人物，殘毒生類，邑人輒出，遂取而殺。擊鼓吹貝，負弩持矛，群從成旅，然後免害。其王懼仁化之不洽也，乃縱獵者，期於擒獲。王躬率四兵，眾以萬計，掩薄林藪，彌跨山谷。師子震吼，人畜僻易。既不擒獲，尋復招募，其有擒執師子除國患者，當酬重賞，式旌茂績。其子聞王之令，乃謂母曰：「飢寒已甚，宜可應募，或有所得，以相撫育。」母曰：「言不可若是！彼雖畜也，猶謂父焉，豈以艱辛，而興逆害？」子曰：「人畜異類，禮義安在？既以違阻，此心何冀？」乃袖小刀，出應招募。是時千眾萬騎，雲屯霧合，師子踞在林中，人莫敢近。子即其前，父遂馴伏，於是乎親愛忘怒，乃剚刃於腹中，尚懷慈愛，猶無忿毒，乃至刳腹，含苦而死。王曰：「斯何人哉，若此之異也？」誘之以福利，震之以威禍，然後具陳始末，備述情事。王曰：「逆哉！父而尚害，況非親乎？畜種難馴，兇情易動。除民之害，其功大矣；斷父之命，其心逆矣。重賞以酬其功，遠放以誅其逆。則國典不虧，王言不二。」於是裝二大船，多儲糧糗。母留在國，周給賞功，子女各從一舟，隨波飄蕩。其男船泛海至此寶渚，見豐珍玉，便於中止。其後商人採寶，復至渚中，乃殺其商主，留其子女。如是繁息，子孫眾多，遂立君臣，以位上下，建都築邑，據有疆域，以其先祖擒執師子，因舉元功，而為國號。其女船者，泛至波剌斯西，神鬼所魅，產育群女，故今西大女國是也。故師子國人形貌卑黑，方頤大顙，情性獷烈，安忍鴆毒，斯亦猛獸遺種，故其人多勇健。斯一說也。佛法所記，則曰：昔此寶洲大鐵城中，五百羅剎女之所居也。城樓之上竪二高幢，表吉凶之相，有吉事吉幢動，有凶事凶幢動。恒伺商人至寶洲者，便變為美女，持香華，奏音樂，出迎慰問，誘入鐵城，樂讌會已，而置鐵牢中，漸取食之。時贍部洲有大商主僧伽者，其子字僧伽羅。父既年老，代知家務，與五百商人入海採寶，風波飄蕩，遇至寶洲。時羅剎女望吉幢動，便齎香華，鼓奏音樂，相携迎候，誘入鐵城。商主於是對羅剎女王歡娛樂會，自餘商侶，各相配合，彌歷歲時，皆生一子。諸羅剎女情疎故人，欲幽之鐵牢，更伺商侶。時僧伽羅夜感惡夢，知非吉祥，竊求歸路，遇至鐵牢，乃聞悲號之聲，遂昇高樹，問曰：「誰相拘縶，而此怨傷？」曰：「爾不知耶？城中諸女，並是羅剎，昔誘我曹入城娛樂。君既將至，幽牢我曹，漸充所食，今已太半，君等不久亦遭此禍。」僧伽羅曰：「當圖何計，可免危難？」對曰：「我聞海濱有一天馬，至誠祈請，必相濟渡。」僧伽羅聞已，竊告商侶，共望海濱，專精求救。是時天馬來告人曰：「爾輩各執我毛鬣，不回顧者，我濟汝曹，越海免難，至贍部洲，吉達鄉國。」諸商人奉指告，專一無二，執其髦鬣，天馬乃騰驤雲路，越濟海岸。諸羅剎女忽覺夫逃，遞相告語，異其所去，各携稚子凌虛往來。知諸商人將出海濱，遂相召命，飛行遠訪。嘗未踰時，遇諸商侶，悲憙俱至，涕淚交流，各掩泣而言曰：「我惟感遇，幸會良人，室家有慶，恩愛已久，而今遠棄，妻子孤遺，悠悠此心，誰其能忍？幸願留顧，相與還城。」商人之心未肯回慮，諸羅剎女策說無功，遂縱妖媚，備行矯惑。商侶愛戀，情難堪忍，心疑去留，身皆退墮。羅剎諸女更相拜賀，與彼商人携持而去。僧伽羅者，智慧深固，心無滯累，得越大海，免斯危難。時羅剎女王空還鐵城，諸女謂曰：「汝無智略，為夫所棄，既寡藝能，宜勿居此。」時羅剎女王持所生子，飛至僧伽羅前，縱極媚惑，誘請令還。僧伽羅口誦神呪，手揮利劍，叱而告曰：「汝是羅剎，我乃是人，人鬼異路，非其匹合。若苦相逼，當斷汝命。」羅剎女知誘惑之不遂也，凌虛而去，至僧伽羅家，詐其父僧伽曰：「我是某國王女，僧伽羅娶我為妻，生一子矣，齎持寶貨，來還鄉國。泛海遭風，舟楫漂沒，唯我子母及僧伽羅，僅而獲濟。山川道阻，凍餧艱辛，一言忤意，遂見棄遺，詈言不遜，罵為羅剎。歸則家國遼遠，止則孤遺覊旅。進退無依，敢陳情事。」僧伽曰：「誠如所言，宜時即入室。」居未久，僧伽羅至。父謂之曰：「何重財寶，而輕妻子？」僧伽羅曰：「此羅剎女也。」則以先事具白父母，而親宗戚屬咸事驅逐。時羅剎女遂以訴王，王欲罪僧伽羅。僧伽羅曰：「羅剎之女，情多妖惑。」王以為不誠也，而情悅其淑美，謂僧伽羅曰：「必棄此女，今留後宮。」僧伽羅曰：「恐為災禍。斯既羅剎，食唯血肉。」王不聽僧伽羅之言，遂納為妻。其後夜分，飛還寶渚，召餘五百羅剎鬼女共至王宮，以毒呪術殘害宮中，凡諸人畜，食肉飲血，持其餘屍，還歸寶渚。旦日群臣朝集，王門閉而不開，候聽久之，不聞人語。於是排其戶，闢其門，相從趨進，遂至宮庭，閴其無人，唯有骸骨。群官僚佐相顧失圖，悲號慟哭，莫測禍源。僧伽羅具告始末，臣庶信然，禍自招矣。於是國輔、老臣、群官、宿將，歷問明德，推據崇高，咸仰僧伽羅之福智也，乃相議曰：「夫君人者，豈苟且哉？先資福智，次體明哲，非福智無以享寶位，非明哲何以理機務？僧伽羅者，斯其人矣。夢察禍機，感應天馬，忠以諫主，智足謀身。曆運在茲，惟新成詠。」眾庶樂推，尊立為王。僧伽羅辭不獲免，允執其中，恭揖群官，遂即王位。於是沿革前弊，表式賢良。乃下令曰：「吾先商侶在羅剎國，死生莫測，善惡不分。今將救難，宜整兵甲，拯危恤患，國之福也；收珍藏寶，國之利也。」於是治兵，浮海而往。時鐵城上凶幢遂動，諸羅剎女覩而惶怖，便縱妖媚，出迎誘誑。王素知其詐，令諸兵士口誦神呪，身奮武威。諸羅剎女蹎墜退敗，或逃隱孤島，或沈溺洪流。於是毀鐵城，破鐵牢，救得商人，多獲珠寶。招募黎庶，遷居寶洲，建都築邑，遂有國焉。因以王名而為國號。僧伽羅者，則釋迦如來本生之事也。僧伽羅國先時唯宗淫祀。佛去世後第一百年，無憂王弟摩醯因陀羅捨離欲愛，志求聖果，得六神通，具八解脫，足步虛空，來遊此國，弘宣正法，流布遺教。自茲已降，風俗淳信。伽藍數百所，僧徒二萬餘人，遵行大乘上座部法。佛教至後二百餘年，各擅專門，分成二部：一曰摩訶毘訶羅住部，斥大乘，習小教。二曰阿跋耶祇釐住部，學兼二乘，弘演三藏。僧徒乃戒行貞潔，定慧凝明，儀範可師，濟濟如也。王宮側有佛牙精舍，高數百尺，瑩以珠珍，飾之奇寶。精舍上建表柱，置鉢曇摩羅加大寶，寶光赫奕，聯暉照曜，晝夜遠望，爛若明星。王以佛牙日三灌洗，香水香末，或濯或焚，務極珍奇，式修供養。佛牙精舍側有小精舍，亦以眾寶而為瑩飾。中有金佛像，此國先王等身而鑄，肉髻則貴寶飾焉。其後有盜，伺欲竊取，而重門周檻，衛守清切。盜乃鑿通孔道，入精舍而穴之，遂欲取寶，像漸高遠。其盜既不果求，退而歎曰：「如來在昔修菩薩行，起廣大心，發弘誓願，上自身命，下至國城，悲愍四生，周給一切。今者，如何遺像悋寶？靜言於此，不明昔行。」像乃俯首而授寶焉。是盜得已，尋持貨賣，人或見者，咸謂之曰：「此寶乃先王金佛像頂髻寶也。爾從何獲，來此鬻賣？」遂擒以白王。王問所從得，盜曰：「佛自與我，我非盜也。」王以為不誠，命使觀驗，像猶俯首。王覩聖靈，信心淳固，不罪其人，重贖其寶，莊嚴像髻，重置頂焉。像因俯首，以至於今。王宮側建大厨，日營萬八千僧食。食時既至，僧徒持鉢受饌，既得食已，各還其居。自佛教流被，建斯供養，子孫承統，繼業至今。十數年來，國中政亂，未有定主，乃廢斯業。國濱海隅，地產珍寶，王親祠祭，神呈奇貨，都人士子，往來求採，稱其福報，所獲不同。隨得珠璣，賦稅有科。
en_current: The country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) is over 7,000 li in circumference. The capital city is over 40 li in circumference. The land is fertile, the climate is warm and hot, crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The population is prosperous, and the households are wealthy. The people are short and dark-skinned, and their temperaments are fierce and impetuous. They are fond of learning and value virtue, honoring goodness and diligently cultivating merit. This country was originally an island of gems; it contains many precious treasures and is inhabited by ghosts and spirits.  Later, there was a king in South India whose daughter was betrothed to a neighboring country. On an auspicious day, as she was being escorted there, they encountered a lion on the road. Her attendants abandoned the girl and fled to escape the danger, but the girl remained in her carriage, resigned to losing her life. At that time, the lion king carried the girl away, entering deep mountains and dwelling in secluded valleys. He hunted deer and gathered fruit to provide for her in due season. After many years had passed, she gave birth to a son and a daughter; their appearance was that of humans, but their nature was that of beasts.   As the son gradually grew up, he had the strength to wrestle with wild beasts. When he reached the age of twenty, his human intelligence began to manifest, and he said to his mother, "What am I? My father is a wild beast, and my mother is a human. Since we are not of the same species, how could they have mated?" His mother then recounted the past to her son. He said, "Humans and beasts follow different paths; we should flee at once." The mother said, "I tried to escape before, but I could not succeed on my own." The son subsequently followed his lion father, climbing mountains and crossing ridges to observe his movements so that they might escape the danger. Once he had waited for his father to leave, he carried his mother and sister on his back and descended toward human settlements. The mother said, "We must each be cautious and secretive; do not speak of the origin of these events, for if people should hear of them, they may look down upon us." Thereupon, they arrived at her father’s native country, but the country was not that of their kin, and their ancestral line had already been extinguished. They sought shelter with the townspeople, who asked them, "From what country are you?" They replied, "We are originally from this country, but we were scattered in foreign lands; mother and son have traveled together to return to our old home." The people all felt pity and compassion, and together they provided them with supplies.  When the lion king returned and saw nothing, he pined for his children. His fury erupted, and he left the mountain valleys to roam among the villages and towns, roaring and thundering, violently harming people and animals, and cruelly destroying living beings. Whenever the townspeople came out, he would seize and kill them. They beat drums and blew conch shells, shouldered crossbows and held spears, and followed in groups like an army; only then could they avoid harm.  The king, fearing that his benevolent influence was not reaching the people, released hunters, hoping to capture the beast. The king personally led the four divisions of the army, numbering in the tens of thousands, to surround the forests and thickets, spanning across the mountains and valleys. The lion roared, and both men and beasts fled in terror. Since he could not be captured, the king subsequently issued a recruitment call: whoever could seize the lion and rid the country of this menace would be rewarded with a great prize to honor their distinguished achievement.  Upon hearing the king’s order, the son said to his mother, "Our hunger and cold have become extreme; I should respond to the recruitment, for perhaps I may gain something with which to support you." The mother said, "You must not speak like this! Although he is a beast, he is still called your father; how could you, because of hardship, commit such an act of rebellion and harm?" The son replied, "Humans and beasts are of different species; where then is the place for ritual and righteousness? Since we are already obstructed and hindered, what hope is there for this heart?" He then hid a small knife in his sleeve and went out to answer the recruitment. At that time, thousands of people and ten thousand cavalry gathered like clouds and mist, but the lion sat in the forest, and no one dared to approach. The son went directly before him, and the father became tame and submissive. Thus, out of affection, he forgot his anger; the son then stabbed his blade into the father’s belly. The father still harbored loving kindness and remained without resentment or malice, even as his belly was ripped open, and he died enduring the pain. The king asked, "What kind of person is this, that he is so extraordinary?" He tempted him with benefits and threatened him with punishment, after which the son fully explained the beginning and the end, detailing the entire situation. The king said, "How rebellious! If he would even harm his own father, how much more so would he harm those who are not his kin? The beast species is difficult to tame, and their violent nature is easily stirred. To remove a menace to the people is a great merit, but to sever the life of one's father is a rebellious heart. I shall provide a heavy reward to compensate for his merit, but I shall banish him far away to punish his rebellion. In this way, the laws of the country will not be compromised, and the king’s word will not be inconsistent." Thereupon, he fitted out two large ships and stored them with plenty of provisions. The mother was left in the country and provided for with the reward for the merit, while the son and daughter were each placed on a ship and left to drift with the waves. The son’s ship drifted across the sea until it reached this island of treasures; seeing an abundance of precious gems, he settled there. Later, when merchants came to the island to collect treasures, he killed the merchant leader and kept his children. In this way they multiplied, and their descendants were numerous. They then established a ruler and ministers, assigned ranks of high and low, built a capital and cities, and occupied the territory. Because their ancestor had captured a lion (siṃha), they cited this original achievement to name the country. As for the ship carrying the daughter, it drifted to the west of Persia (Pārasī), where she was bewitched by spirits and gave birth to a group of daughters; this is the origin of the present-day Western Kingdom of Women. Therefore, the people of the country of the Lion (Siṃhala) are short and dark in appearance, with square chins and broad foreheads; their temperament is fierce and violent, and they are cruel and prone to poisoning. This is because they are the descendants of a wild beast, and thus the people are mostly brave and robust. This is one account.  What the Buddha’s teaching records is as follows: In the past, in the great iron city of this precious island, there dwelt five hundred rākṣasīs. Atop the city towers, two tall banners were erected to signify signs of good or ill fortune; the auspicious banner would move when there was a lucky event, and the inauspicious banner would move when there was a calamity. They would constantly lie in wait for merchants arriving at the precious island, whereupon they would transform into beautiful women, carrying fragrant flowers and playing music to welcome and console them, luring them into the iron city. After the festivities and banquets were over, they would place the merchants in an iron prison and gradually devour them.  At that time, in the continent of Jambudvīpa, there was a great merchant leader named Saṃgha; his son was named Saṃghala. His father being old, he took over the family business and set out with five hundred merchants to enter the sea to collect treasures. Blown about by wind and waves, they happened to reach the precious island. When the rākṣasīs saw the auspicious banner move, they brought fragrant flowers and played music, coming together to welcome the merchants and entice them into the iron city. The merchant leader then engaged in joyful entertainment with the rākṣasī queen, and the remaining merchants each paired off with one, and as the years passed, they all fathered children. The rākṣasīs, their affections for their old partners having grown distant, wished to imprison them in an iron jail to wait for other merchants. At that time, Saṃghala had a nightmare during the night and, knowing it was not an auspicious sign, secretly sought a path home. He happened upon the iron jail and heard the sound of piteous wailing, so he climbed a tall tree and asked, "Who is it that is bound and suffering such grief?" They replied, "Do you not know? The women in the city are all rākṣasīs. In the past, they enticed us into the city for entertainment. Once you had arrived, they imprisoned us and gradually consumed us as food; now more than half are gone, and before long, you too will suffer this same calamity." Saṃghala asked, "What plan can be devised to escape this danger?" They replied, "We have heard that there is a heavenly horse on the seashore; if one prays with utmost sincerity, it will surely ferry one across to safety." Having heard this, Saṃghala secretly informed the other merchants, and together they looked toward the seashore, focusing their minds on seeking salvation. At that time, the heavenly horse came and told the men, "If each of you grasps my mane and does not look back, I will ferry you across the sea to escape this peril and reach the continent of Jambudvīpa, returning to your home country." The merchants followed these instructions with single-minded devotion and gripped its mane; the heavenly horse then soared into the clouds and galloped across the seacoast. The rākṣasīs (羅剎女) suddenly realized their husbands had fled; they told one another, wondering where they had gone, and each carrying her young child, they flew through the air in search of them. Knowing the merchants were about to reach the seashore, they called out to one another and flew off to find them. Before long, they encountered the company of merchants; with mixed feelings of grief and joy, their tears flowed freely as they covered their faces, sobbing and saying: "I am grateful for our meeting and fortunate to have wed such a fine man; our home was full of joy and we have long shared deep affection, yet now you abandon us to go far away, leaving your wife and child desolate—how can anyone endure such a heart-wrenching fate? We pray you, look back and return with us to the city."  The hearts of the merchants remained unmoved. The rākṣasīs, finding their entreaties of no avail, resorted to their demonic charms and employed every manner of deception. The merchants, overcome by love and unable to bear the separation, felt their resolve waver, and they all fell back. The rākṣasīs congratulated one another and went away, holding the merchants by the hand.  Siṃhala (僧伽羅), however, possessed deep and firm wisdom; his mind was free from attachments, and he succeeded in crossing the great sea, escaping this peril. Meanwhile, the queen of the rākṣasīs returned alone to the Iron City. The other rākṣasīs said to her, "You lack wisdom and strategy, having been abandoned by your husband; since you are devoid of skill and ability, you should no longer dwell here."  The queen of the rākṣasīs then took the child she had borne, flew before Siṃhala, and, exerting her utmost charms, enticed and pleaded with him to return. Siṃhala recited a mantra and, brandishing his sharp sword, rebuked her, saying: "You are a rākṣasī, and I am a human; humans and ghosts follow different paths, and we are not a match. If you press me hard, I shall end your life." The rākṣasī, knowing that her seduction had failed, flew through the air and arrived at the home of Siṃhala (僧伽羅). She deceived his father, Siṃha (僧伽), saying: "I am the daughter of a certain king. Siṃhala took me as his wife and we bore a son. We were carrying precious goods to return to his native country, but while crossing the sea, we encountered a storm and our ship was wrecked. Only my son, myself, and Siṃhala managed to survive. The mountains and rivers were difficult to traverse, and we suffered from cold, hunger, and hardship. Because of one word that displeased him, I was abandoned and cast aside, insulted with improper language, and reviled as a rākṣasī. To return home is to face a vast distance, and to stay here is to be a lonely, stranded traveler. With nowhere to turn, I dare to present my situation."  Siṃha said, "It is truly as you say; you should enter the house at once." Not long after, Siṃhala arrived. His father said to him, "Why do you value wealth and treasure while slighting your wife and child?" Siṃhala replied, "This is a rākṣasī." He then explained the previous events in detail to his parents, and his relatives and kin all joined in driving her away.  The rākṣasī then complained to the king, and the king wished to punish Siṃhala. Siṃhala said, "She is a rākṣasī, and her nature is full of seductive bewitchment." The king believed this was untrue, and being charmed by her beauty, he said to Siṃhala, "If you must abandon this woman, I shall keep her in my harem." Siṃhala replied, "I fear it will bring disaster. Since she is a rākṣasī, her only food is blood and flesh." The king did not listen to the words of Siṃhala and proceeded to take her as his wife. Later, in the middle of the night, she flew back to the precious island (Ratnadvīpa) and summoned the other five hundred rākṣasī demonesses to come together to the royal palace. Using poisonous incantations, they ravaged the palace; they ate the flesh and drank the blood of all the people and animals, then took the remaining corpses and returned to the precious island. At daybreak, the ministers and officials gathered for court, but the palace gates were closed and would not open. They waited and listened for a long time, but heard no human voices. Thereupon, they pushed against the doors and opened the gates, following one another as they hurried inside. When they reached the palace courtyard, it was silent and empty of people; there were only skeletons. The officials and aides looked at one another in dismay, wailing and weeping, unable to fathom the source of the disaster. Siṃhala recounted the entire story from beginning to end, and the ministers and subjects believed him, realizing that the king had brought this disaster upon himself.  Thereupon, the state assistants, veteran ministers, various officials, and senior generals inquired after those of illustrious virtue and sought out those of sublime character; all admired the merit and wisdom of Siṃhala, and they consulted together, saying: "How can the one who rules the people be chosen haphazardly? He must first possess merit and wisdom, and secondly embody sagacity and discernment; for without merit and wisdom, one cannot enjoy the precious throne, and without sagacity and discernment, how can one manage the affairs of state? Siṃhala is the very man. He perceived the hidden danger in a dream, was moved by the response of the heavenly horse, was loyal in remonstrating with his lord, and was wise enough to protect himself. The mandate of history is here; let us compose a new song of praise." The masses were happy to support him and honored him by establishing him as king. Siṃhala, unable to decline the offer, agreed to hold to the middle path, and after bowing respectfully to the assembled officials, he ascended the throne. Thereupon, he reformed the previous abuses and set an example of virtue. He then issued an order, saying: "Our former merchant companions are in the land of the Rākṣasas; their life or death is uncertain, and good and evil are indistinguishable. Now, to rescue them from their plight, we should prepare our arms and armor; to save those in peril and show compassion to those in distress is a blessing to the state; to recover precious goods and store up treasures is a benefit to the state." Thereupon, he organized his troops and traveled across the sea. At that time, the banners of ill omen atop the iron city began to shake; the Rākṣasīs, seeing this, were struck with terror and immediately unleashed their seductive charms, coming out to meet the men to entice and deceive them. The king, having long known of their deceit, ordered his soldiers to recite mantras with their mouths and exert their martial might with their bodies. The Rākṣasīs stumbled, fell, and were defeated; some fled to hide on isolated islands, while others drowned in the surging currents. Thereupon, he destroyed the iron city, broke the iron prisons, rescued the merchants, and obtained many jewels. He recruited the common people to move and settle on the treasure island, established a capital, built towns, and thus a kingdom was formed. He then used the king’s name as the name of the country.  Siṃhala (僧伽羅) is a matter from a previous life of Śākya Tathāgata. In earlier times, the kingdom of Siṃhala only honored licentious sacrifices. In the hundredth year after the Buddha passed away, Mahendra (摩醯因陀羅), the younger brother of King Aśoka (無憂王), abandoned worldly desires to seek the fruits of sainthood; having attained the six supernatural powers and the eight liberations, he traveled through the air to this country to propagate the true Dharma and spread the bequeathed teachings. From that time onward, the customs have been pure and faithful. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas and over twenty thousand monks, who follow the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. More than two hundred years after the arrival of Buddhism, each [group] specialized in its own field, dividing into two schools: the first is the Mahāvihāra (摩訶毘訶羅) school, which rejects the Mahāyāna and studies the Lesser Vehicle; the second is the Abhayagiri (阿跋耶祇釐) school, which studies both vehicles and propagates the Tripiṭaka. The monks are pure in their moral conduct, their concentration and wisdom are clear and bright, their deportment is exemplary, and they are numerous and flourishing.  Beside the royal palace is the Temple of the Buddha’s Tooth (佛牙精舍), several hundred feet high, shimmering with pearls and adorned with rare gems. A signal post is erected atop the temple, upon which is placed a large padmarāga jewel; its brilliant light shines resplendently, and when viewed from afar, it glitters like a bright star by day or night. Three times a day, the king bathes the Buddha’s tooth with scented water and powdered incense, either washing it or burning the incense, striving for the utmost rarity and splendor in his offerings.  Beside the Temple of the Buddha’s Tooth is a small temple, which is also adorned and polished with various precious gems. Inside is a golden Buddha statue, cast by a former king of this country to be of equal stature to himself, with the uṣṇīṣa adorned with precious jewels. Later, there was a thief who waited for an opportunity to steal it, but the heavy doors and surrounding railings were guarded with strict vigilance. The thief then dug a tunnel to enter the temple through a hole; when he attempted to take the jewel, the statue gradually grew taller and higher. Having failed in his quest, the thief retreated and sighed, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata practiced the bodhisattva path, aroused a vast mind, and made great vows, offering up his own life and body, down to his cities and kingdoms, out of compassion for the four types of birth, bestowing everything upon all beings. Now, how could his bequeathed image be stingy with a jewel?" "Reflecting on this, I do not understand the past conduct." The image then bowed its head and bestowed the jewel. Having obtained it, the thief immediately took it to sell. Those who saw it all said to him, "This treasure is the jewel from the *uṣṇīṣa* (頂髻) of the golden Buddha image of the former king. Where did you obtain it to come here and sell it?" They then seized him and reported it to the king. The king asked where he had obtained it, and the thief said, "The Buddha gave it to me himself; I am not a thief." The king, thinking he was not being truthful, ordered an envoy to go and verify it, and the image was still bowing its head. Witnessing this sacred miracle, the king’s faith became pure and firm; he did not punish the man, but instead redeemed the jewel at a high price, adorned the image’s *uṣṇīṣa*, and replaced it on the crown. Because of this, the image has remained with its head bowed until the present day.  Beside the royal palace, a great kitchen was built, preparing food for eighteen thousand monks daily. When the time for the meal arrived, the assembly of monks would hold their alms bowls to receive the provisions, and having received their food, each would return to his own residence. Since the time the Buddha’s teaching spread to this land, this offering was established, and descendants inherited the succession, continuing the practice until the present. For the past ten or more years, the country has been in political turmoil without a stable ruler, and this practice has been abandoned. The country is situated on the edge of the sea and the land produces precious gems. When the king personally performs sacrifices, the spirits present rare treasures. The city’s inhabitants and scholars travel back and forth to seek and collect them, and according to their karmic rewards, what they obtain differs. Depending on the pearls and gems they acquire, there is a set tax.

zh: 佛教至後二百餘年，各擅專門，分成二部：一曰摩訶毘訶羅住部，斥大乘，習小教。
en_current: More than two hundred years after the arrival of Buddhism, each [group] specialized in its own field, and they divided into two schools: the first is called the Mahāvihāra school (摩訶毘訶羅住部), which rejects the Mahāyāna and studies the Hīnayāna teachings.

zh: 二曰阿跋耶祇釐住部，學兼二乘，弘演三藏。
en_current: The second is the Abhayagiri-vihāra school (阿跋耶祇釐住部), which studies both vehicles and propagates the Tripiṭaka.

zh: 國南浮海數千里，至那羅稽羅洲。洲人卑小，長餘三尺，人身鳥喙，既無穀稼，唯食椰子。
en_current: Sailing several thousand li across the sea to the south of the country, one reaches the island of Nārikela (那羅稽羅洲). The inhabitants of the island are diminutive, being just over three feet tall; they have human bodies and bird-like beaks, and as they do not cultivate grain or crops, they subsist solely on coconuts.

zh: 那羅稽羅洲西浮海數千里，孤島東崖有石佛像，高百餘尺，東面坐，以月愛珠為肉髻，月將回照，水即懸流，滂霈崖嶺，臨注谿壑。時有商侶，遭風飄浪，隨波泛濫，遂至孤島，海鹹不可以飲，渴乏者久之。是時月十五日也，像頂流水，眾皆獲濟，以為至誠所感，靈聖拯之。於即留停，遂經數日，每月隱高巖，其水不流。時商主曰：「未必為濟我曹而流水也。嘗聞月愛珠月光照即水流注耳，將非佛像頂上有此寶耶？」遂登崖而視之，乃以月愛珠為像肉髻。當見其人，說其始末。
en_current: Sailing several thousand *li* west across the sea from the country of Nārikela (那羅稽羅洲), on the eastern cliff of a solitary island, there is a stone Buddha statue over a hundred feet high, seated facing east. It has a moonstone (*candrakānta*) as its *uṣṇīṣa*; when the moon shines upon it, water flows down, drenching the cliffs and ridges and pouring into the mountain ravines. At one time, a group of merchants, having encountered a storm and drifted with the waves, arrived at this solitary island. The sea water was salty and undrinkable, and they suffered from thirst for a long time. It happened to be the fifteenth day of the month, and water flowed from the top of the statue, by which the entire group was saved; they believed that their utmost sincerity had moved the divine sage to rescue them. They remained there for several days, but whenever the moon was hidden behind the high cliffs, the water would not flow. The leader of the merchants then said, "It is not necessarily the case that it flows to save us. I have heard that when moonlight shines upon a moonstone, water will flow; could it be that there is such a gem atop the head of the Buddha statue?" They then climbed the cliff to look at it and found that the *uṣṇīṣa* of the image was indeed made of moonstone. When they met the people there, they told them the whole story from beginning to end.

zh: 國西浮海數千里，至大寶洲，無人居止，唯神棲宅。靜夜遙望，光燭山水。商人往之者多矣，咸無所得。
en_current: To the west of the country, sailing several thousand li across the sea, one reaches the Great Treasure Island (Mahāratnadvīpa), which is uninhabited by humans and serves only as an abode for deities. In the quiet of the night, looking from afar, its light illuminates the mountains and waters. Many merchants have traveled there, but all have returned without obtaining anything.

zh: 國東南隅有䮚（勒鄧反）迦山，巖谷幽峻，神鬼遊舍，在昔如來於此說《䮚迦經》（舊曰楞伽經，訛也）。
en_current: In the southeastern corner of the country is Mount Laṅkā (䮚迦山) (䮚 is pronounced by the *fanqie* 勒鄧), with its steep cliffs and deep valleys where spirits and ghosts dwell; it is here that the Tathāgata formerly preached the Laṅkā Sūtra (the old name, Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra [楞伽經], is an error).

zh: 自達羅毘荼國北入林野中，歷孤城，過小邑，凶人結黨，作害覊旅。行二千餘里，至荼建那補羅國（南印度境）。荼建那補羅國，周五千餘里。國大都城周三十餘里。土地膏腴，稼穡滋盛。氣序溫暑，風俗躁烈。形貌黧黑，情性獷暴。好學業，尚德藝。伽藍百餘所，僧徒萬餘人，大小二乘，兼功綜習。天祠數百，異道雜居。王宮城側有大伽藍，僧徒三百餘人，寔唯俊彥也。其伽藍大精舍高百餘尺，中有一切義成太子寶冠，高減二尺，飾以寶珍，盛以寶函。每至齋日，出置高座，香花供養，時放光明。城側大伽藍中有精舍，高五十餘尺，中有刻檀慈氏菩薩像，高十餘尺，或至齋日，神光照燭，是聞二百億羅漢之所造也。城北不遠有多羅樹林，周三十餘里，其葉長廣，其色光潤，諸國書寫，莫不採用。林中有窣堵波，是過去四佛坐及經行遺跡之所。其側則有聞二百億羅漢遺身舍利窣堵波也。城東不遠有窣堵波，基已傾陷，餘高三丈。聞諸先志曰：此中有如來舍利，或至齋日，時燭靈光。在昔如來於此說法，現神通力，度諸群生。城西南不遠有窣堵波，高百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。是聞二百億羅漢於此現大神通，化度眾生。傍有伽藍，唯餘基趾，是彼羅漢之所建也。
en_current: From the country of Draviḍa (達羅毘荼國), traveling north into the forests and wilderness, passing isolated cities and small towns where bands of brigands harm travelers, one journeys over two thousand *li* to reach the country of Konkaṇapura (荼建那補羅國) (in the region of South India). The country of Konkaṇapura is over five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circuit. The land is fertile and crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are impetuous and fierce. The people are dark-complexioned and their temperaments are wild and violent. They are fond of learning and value virtue and the arts. There are over one hundred monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are several hundred *deva* temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Beside the royal palace is a large monastery with over three hundred monks, who are truly men of outstanding talent. In the great *vihāra* (精舍) of this monastery, which is over one hundred feet high, is the precious crown of Prince Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成太子). It is slightly less than two feet high, adorned with precious jewels, and kept in a jeweled casket. Whenever a fast day arrives, it is brought out and placed on a high seat to be worshipped with incense and flowers, and at times it emits a brilliant light. Beside the city, in a large monastery, there is a *vihāra* over fifty feet high, containing a sandalwood statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩) over ten feet tall. On fast days, it sometimes shines with a divine light; it was made by the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (聞二百億羅漢). Not far to the north of the city is a forest of *tāla* trees, over thirty *li* in circuit. Its leaves are long and broad, and their color is glossy and smooth; all the various countries use them for writing. In the forest there is a stūpa, which is the site of the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the four past Buddhas. Beside it is a stūpa containing the bodily relics of the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi. Not far to the east of the city is a stūpa; its base has already collapsed and sunk, and it remains three *zhang* high. According to ancient records, it contains relics of the Tathāgata, and on fast days it sometimes shines with a divine light. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here and manifested his supernatural powers to save the multitudes of living beings. Not far to the southwest of the city is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It is here that the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi manifested great supernatural powers here to transform and save living beings. Beside it is a monastery, of which only the foundations remain, which was built by that Arhat.

zh: 從此西北入大林野，猛獸暴害，群盜兇殘。行二千四五百里，至摩訶剌侘國（南印度境）。摩訶剌侘國，周六千餘里。國大都城西臨大河，周三十餘里。土地沃壤，稼穡殷盛。氣序溫暑，風俗淳質。其形偉大，其性傲逸，有恩必報，有怨必復，人或陵辱，殉命以讎，窘急投分，忘身以濟。將復怨也，必先告之，各被堅甲，然後爭鋒。臨陣逐北，不殺已降。兵將失利，無所刑罰，賜之女服，感激自死。國養勇士，有數百人，每將決戰，飲酒酣醉，一人摧鋒，萬夫挫銳。遇人肆害，國刑不加，每出遊行，擊鼓前導。復𩚅暴象，凡數百頭，將欲陣戰，亦先飲酒，群馳蹈踐，前無堅敵。其王恃此人象，輕陵隣國。王，剎帝利種也，名補羅稽舍。謀猷弘遠，仁慈廣被，臣下事之，盡其忠矣。今戒日大王東征西伐，遠賓邇肅，唯此國人獨不臣伏，屢率五印度甲兵，及募召諸國烈將，躬往討伐，猶未克勝。其兵也如此，其俗也如彼。人知好學，邪正兼崇。伽藍百餘所，僧徒五千餘人，大小二乘，兼功綜習。天祠百數，異道甚多。大城內外，五窣堵波，並過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所，無憂王建也。自餘石甎諸窣堵波，其數甚多，難用備舉。城南不遠有故伽藍，中有觀自在菩薩石像，靈鑒潛被，願求多果。
en_current: From here, traveling northwest into a great forest and wilderness, one encounters ferocious beasts and cruel bands of robbers. After traveling two thousand four or five hundred li, one reaches the country of Mahārāṣṭra (摩訶剌侘國) (in the territory of South India). The country of Mahārāṣṭra is over six thousand li in circumference. The capital city borders a great river on the west and is over thirty li in circumference. The soil is fertile and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are simple and honest. The people are tall and sturdy in stature and proud and carefree by nature; they never fail to repay a kindness or avenge a grievance. If someone insults them, they will risk their lives to take vengeance; if someone is in desperate straits and seeks their aid, they will forget their own safety to assist them. When they intend to take revenge, they must first notify their opponent; both sides then don sturdy armor before engaging in battle. When pursuing a retreating enemy on the battlefield, they do not kill those who have surrendered. If a general or soldier suffers a defeat, he is not punished; instead, he is presented with women’s clothing, and, feeling ashamed, he will take his own life. The state maintains several hundred warriors. Whenever they are about to engage in a decisive battle, they drink until they are intoxicated; a single one of these men can break the vanguard, causing ten thousand men to lose their edge. If they happen to harm someone, the state does not impose punishment; whenever they go out, they have drums beaten to lead the way. Furthermore, they keep several hundred ferocious elephants. When they are about to engage in battle, these elephants are also given wine to drink; they then charge in a group, trampling everything, with no firm enemy able to stand before them. The king relies on these men and elephants to lightly treat and bully neighboring countries. The king is of the Kṣatriya (剎帝利) caste and is named Pulakeśin (補羅稽舍). His strategies and plans are far-reaching, and his benevolence is widely extended; his subjects serve him with the utmost loyalty. Currently, the great King Śīlāditya (戒日大王) campaigns from the east to the west, bringing distant lands to submission and near lands to order; only the people of this country alone refuse to acknowledge his suzerainty. Although he has repeatedly led the armored troops of the Five Indias and summoned the heroic generals of many nations to personally lead an invasion, he has yet to achieve victory. Such is their military, and such are their customs. The people are known for their love of learning, and they revere both the heterodox and the orthodox. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with more than five thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are hundreds of Deva temples, and the heterodox sects are very numerous. Inside and outside the great city, there are five stūpas (窣堵波), all of which are sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). As for the other stone and brick stūpas, their number is so great that it is difficult to enumerate them all. Not far to the south of the city is an old saṃghārāma, in which there is a stone image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩); its spiritual efficacy is secretly felt, and those who pray for wishes often see them fulfilled.

zh: 國東境有大山，疊嶺連障，重巒絕巘。爰有伽藍，基于幽谷，高堂邃宇，疏崖枕峯，重閣層臺，背巖面𭐋，阿折羅（唐言所行）阿羅漢所建。羅漢，西印度人也，其母既終，觀生何趣，見於此國受女人身，羅漢遂來至此，將欲導化，隨機攝受。入里乞食，至母生家，女子持食來施，乳便流汁，親屬既見，以為不祥。羅漢說本因緣，女子便證聖果。羅漢感生育之恩，懷業緣之致，將酬厚德，建此伽藍。伽藍大精舍高百餘尺，中有石佛像，高七十餘尺。上有石蓋七重，虛懸無綴，蓋間相去各三尺餘。聞諸先志曰：斯乃羅漢願力之所持也；或曰神通之力；或曰藥術之功。考厥實錄，未詳其致。精舍四周彫鏤石壁，作如來在昔修菩薩行諸因地事。證聖果之禎祥，入寂滅之靈應，巨細無遺，備盡鐫鏤。伽藍門外，南、北、左、右各一石象。聞之土俗曰：此象時大聲吼，地為震動。昔陳那菩薩多止此伽藍。
en_current: On the eastern border of the country is a great mountain with overlapping ridges and connected barriers, and layered peaks with sheer cliffs. There is a monastery situated in a deep valley, with lofty halls and spacious chambers built against the cliffs and peaks; its multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces lean against the rocks and face the gully. It was built by the Arhat Ācāra (which means "the one who acts" in the language of the Tang). The Arhat was a man from West India. After his mother passed away, he observed where she had been reborn and saw that she had taken a woman's body in this country. The Arhat then came to this place, intending to guide and transform her, accepting her according to her capacity. He entered the village to beg for food and arrived at the house where his mother had been reborn. When the girl brought food to offer as alms, her milk began to flow; when her relatives saw this, they considered it an ill omen. The Arhat explained the original karmic causes, and the woman then attained the holy fruit. Feeling gratitude for the grace of his birth and cherishing the karmic conditions that brought it about, the Arhat built this monastery to repay her profound virtue. The great vihāra (精舍) of the monastery is over a hundred feet high, and within it is a stone Buddha statue more than seventy feet tall. Above it are seven stone canopies, suspended in the void without any attachments, with a space of more than three feet between each canopy. I have heard from the records of those before me that this is sustained by the power of the Arhat’s vows; others say it is by the power of supernatural faculties; still others say it is the work of medicinal arts. Upon examining the actual records, the cause remains unclear. The four walls of the vihara are carved with stone reliefs depicting the various causal deeds of the Tathāgata when he was formerly practicing the Bodhisattva path. The auspicious signs of his attainment of the holy fruit and the spiritual responses upon his entry into nirvana are all carved in detail, leaving nothing out. Outside the gate of the monastery, there is a stone elephant at each of the four positions: south, north, left, and right. According to the local people, these elephants occasionally roar loudly, causing the earth to tremble. In the past, the Bodhisattva Dignāga (陳那) frequently resided in this monastery.

zh: 自此西行千餘里，渡耐秣陀河，至跋祿羯呫（昌葉反）婆國（南印度境）。跋祿羯呫婆國，周二千四五百里。國大都城周二十餘里。土地鹹鹵，草木稀疎。煮海為鹽，利海為業。氣序暑熱，回風颷起。土俗澆薄，人性詭詐。不知學藝，邪正兼信。伽藍十餘所，僧徒三百餘人，習學大乘上座部法。天祠十餘所，異道雜居。
en_current: From here, traveling west for over a thousand li and crossing the Narmada River (耐秣陀河), one reaches the country of Bharukacchapa (跋祿羯呫婆國) (呫 is pronounced by the *fanqie* 昌葉) (in the region of South India). The country of Bharukacchapa is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city is over twenty li in circuit. The land is saline and barren, with sparse vegetation. The people boil seawater to make salt and rely on the sea for their livelihood. The climate is hot, and swirling winds rise up frequently. The local customs are mean and thin, and the people’s nature is deceitful and cunning. They do not study arts or crafts, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten sanghārāmas (伽藍) with over three hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. There are more than ten deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together.

zh: 從此西北行二千餘里，至摩臘婆國（即南羅國。南印度境）。摩臘婆國，周六千餘里。國大都城周三十餘里，據莫醯河東南。土地膏腴，稼穡殷盛，草木榮茂，花菓繁實，特宜宿麥，多食餅麨。人性善順，大抵聰敏，言辭雅亮，學藝優深。五印度境，兩國重學，西南摩臘婆國，東北摩揭陀國，貴德尚仁，明敏強學。而此國也，邪正雜信。伽藍數百所，僧徒二萬餘人，習學小乘正量部法。天祠數百，異道寔眾，多是塗灰之侶也。國志曰：六十年前，王號尸羅阿迭多（唐言戒日）。機慧高明，才學贍敏，愛育四生，敬崇三寶。始自誕靈，洎乎沒齒，貌無瞋色，手不害生。象馬飲水，漉而後𩚅，恐傷水性也。其仁慈如此。在位五十餘年，野獸狎人，舉國黎庶咸不殺害。居宮之側建立精舍，窮諸工巧，備盡莊嚴，中作七佛世尊之像。每歲恒設無遮大會，招集四方僧徒，修施四事供養，或以三衣道具，或以七寶珍奇。奕世相承，美業無替。
en_current: From here, traveling northwest for more than two thousand li, one reaches the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國) (that is, the country of Southern Lāṭa (南羅); within the borders of South India). The country of Mālava is more than six thousand li in circumference. The capital city is more than thirty li in circumference and is situated to the southeast of the Mahī River. The land is fertile, agriculture is flourishing, the vegetation is lush, and flowers and fruits are abundant. It is particularly suitable for winter wheat, and the people eat mostly cakes and parched grain. The nature of the people is gentle and compliant; they are generally intelligent, their speech is elegant and clear, and their learning and arts are profound. Within the borders of the Five Indias, two countries place great importance on learning: the country of Mālava in the southwest and the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) in the northeast; they value virtue, honor benevolence, and are brilliant and diligent in their studies. However, in this country, both heterodox and orthodox beliefs are practiced. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas with more than twenty thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sammatiya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are several hundred deva temples, and the number of heterodox practitioners is substantial; most of them are followers who smear themselves with ashes. The local records state: sixty years ago, there was a king named Śīlāditya (in Chinese, "Sun of Virtue" (戒日)). His ingenuity and wisdom were brilliant, his talent and learning were vast and sharp, he cherished and nurtured the four types of living beings, and he revered and honored the Three Jewels. From his birth until his death, his countenance never showed anger, and his hands never harmed a living creature. When his elephants and horses drank water, he would have it filtered first, fearing that he might injure the life-force of the water. His benevolence was such as this. During his reign of more than fifty years, wild beasts became familiar with humans, and the people of the entire country refrained from killing. Beside the palace, he built a *vihāra* (精舍) with the utmost craftsmanship and exquisite adornment, and within it were fashioned images of the seven World-Honored Buddhas. Every year, he regularly held a great unrestricted assembly (無遮大會, *mokṣa-mahāpariṣad*), gathering monks from all directions to provide them with the four monastic requisites, whether in the form of the three robes and religious implements, or various rare treasures of the seven precious gems. This tradition has been passed down through successive generations, and this noble practice has never ceased.

zh: 大城西北二十餘里，至婆羅門邑，傍有陷坑，秋夏淫滯，彌淹旬日，雖納眾流，而無積水。其傍又建小窣堵波。聞諸先志曰：昔者大慢婆羅門生身陷入地獄之處。昔此邑中，有婆羅門，生知博物，學冠時彥；內外典籍，究極幽微，曆數玄文，若視諸掌；風範清高，令問遐被。王甚珍敬，國人宗重。門人千數，味道欽風。每而言曰：「吾為世出，述聖導凡，先賢後哲，無與我比。彼大自在天、婆藪天、那羅延天、佛世尊者，人皆風靡，祖述其道，莫不圖形，競修祇敬。我今德踰於彼，名擅於時，不有所異，其何以顯？」遂用赤栴檀刻作大自在天、婆藪天、那羅延天、佛世尊等像。為座四足，凡有所至，負以自隨，其慢傲也如此。時西印度有苾芻跋陀羅縷支（唐言賢愛），妙極因明，深窮異論，道風淳粹，戒香郁烈，少欲知足，無求於物，聞而歎曰：「惜哉！時無人矣。令彼愚夫，敢行兇德。」於是荷錫遠遊，來至此國，以其宿心，具白於王。王見弊服，心未之敬，然高其志，強為之禮。遂設論座，告婆羅門曰。婆羅門聞而笑曰：「彼何人斯，敢懷此志？」命其徒屬，來就論場，數百千眾，前後侍聽。賢愛服弊故衣，敷草而坐。彼婆羅門踞所持座，非斥正法，敷述邪宗。苾芻清辯若流，循環往復。婆羅門久而謝屈。王乃謂曰：「久濫虛名，罔上惑眾，先典有記，論負當戮。」欲以鑪鐵，令其坐上。婆羅門窘迫，乃歸命求救。賢愛愍之，乃請王曰：「大王仁禮遠洽，頌聲載途，當布慈育，勿行殘酷，恕其不逮，唯所去就。」王令乘驢，巡告城邑。婆羅門恥其戮辱，發憤歐血。苾芻聞已，往慰之曰：「爾學苞內外，聲聞遐邇，榮辱之事，進退當明。夫名者，何實乎？」婆羅門憤恚，深詈苾芻，謗毀大乘，輕蔑先聖。言聲未靜，地便拆裂，生身墜陷，遺迹斯在。
en_current: More than twenty *li* northwest of the great city, one arrives at the Brahmin village (Brāhmaṇagrāma). Nearby is a deep pit; during the autumn and summer, despite heavy and persistent rains that last for ten days, and although it receives many streams, the water never accumulates. Beside it, a small stūpa has been built. According to ancient records, this is the place where a highly arrogant Brahmin fell into hell while still alive. Formerly, in this village, there was a Brahmin who was naturally wise and widely learned, his scholarship surpassing that of the eminent men of his time. He had thoroughly investigated the profound mysteries of both internal and external scriptures, and the abstruse texts of astronomy and mathematics were as clear to him as if he were looking at the palm of his own hand. His character was noble and refined, and his reputation spread far and wide. The king held him in great esteem and respect, and the people of the country honored him. He had thousands of disciples who admired his way and were drawn to his influence. He would often say, "I have appeared in this world to expound the sacred and guide the ordinary; neither the sages of the past nor the philosophers of the future can compare to me. People are all swept up in following Maheśvara, Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, and the World-Honored Buddha; they propagate their doctrines, paint their images, and vie with one another to offer them worship. Now, since my virtue exceeds theirs and my fame dominates the age, if I do not do something different, how can I manifest my greatness?" He then used red sandalwood to carve images of Maheśvara, Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, and the World-Honored Buddha. He made them the four legs of his seat, and wherever he went, he carried it with him. Such was his arrogance. At that time, in Western India, there was a bhikṣu named Bhadraruci (in Chinese, "Virtuous Love" [賢愛]), who had attained the pinnacle of *hetuvidyā* (logic) and had deeply exhausted the study of heterodox doctrines. His moral conduct was pure and refined, the fragrance of his precepts was intense, and he was possessed of few desires and contentment, seeking nothing from the world. Upon hearing of this, he sighed and said, "Alas! The times are devoid of men, allowing that foolish fellow to dare to practice such wicked deeds." Thereupon, he shouldered his khakkhara (monk's staff) and traveled from afar, arriving in this country, where he fully explained his long-held intention to the king. When the king saw his tattered robes, he did not feel much respect in his heart, yet he esteemed his ambition and reluctantly accorded him the proper courtesies. He then set up a debate seat and informed the Brahmin. The Brahmin heard this and laughed, saying, "Who is that person, that he dares to harbor such an ambition?" He ordered his followers to come to the debate arena, and hundreds of thousands of people gathered before and behind to listen. Bhadraruci wore his tattered, old robes and spread out grass to sit upon. The Brahmin sat perched upon the seat he had brought, denouncing the true Dharma and expounding his heterodox doctrines. The bhikṣu’s clear eloquence flowed like a stream, circling back and forth in argument. After a long time, the Brahmin admitted defeat. The king then said to him, "You have long abused a false reputation, deceiving your superiors and confusing the masses. The ancient codes record that one who loses a debate must be executed." He intended to use a red-hot iron seat to make him sit upon it. The Brahmin, in dire straits, surrendered and begged for his life. Bhadraruci took pity on him and petitioned the king, saying, "Great King, your benevolence and propriety are known far and wide, and your praises fill the roads; you should spread compassionate nurturance rather than practicing cruelty. Forgive his inadequacies and let him go as he pleases." The king ordered him to ride a donkey and announce his defeat throughout the city and its suburbs. The Brahmin, ashamed of this humiliation, became enraged and vomited blood. Upon hearing of this, the bhikṣu went to comfort him, saying, "Your learning encompasses both internal and external doctrines, and your reputation is known far and wide; you should clearly understand the nature of honor and disgrace, and when to advance or retreat. As for fame, what reality does it possess?" The Brahmin, filled with resentment, bitterly reviled the bhikṣu, slandered the Mahāyāna, and spoke with contempt of the ancient sages. Before his words had even died away, the earth split asunder, and he fell alive into the pit; the traces of this event still remain.

zh: 自此西南入海交，西北行二千四五百里，至阿吒釐國（南印度境）。阿吒釐國，周六千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里。居人殷盛，珍寶盈積，稼穡雖備，興販為業。土地沙鹵，花菓稀少。出胡椒樹，樹葉若蜀椒也。出薰陸香樹，樹葉若棠梨也。氣序熱，多風埃。人性澆薄，貴財賤德。文字語言，儀形法則，大同摩臘婆國。多不信福，縱有信者，宗事天神。祠館十餘所，異道雜居。
en_current: From here, traveling southwest into a maritime bay and then northwest for two thousand four or five hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Aṭali (阿吒釐國) (within the borders of South India). The country of Aṭali is more than six thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and precious treasures are accumulated in abundance. Although agriculture is practiced, the people make their living through trade. The land is sandy and saline, and flowers and fruits are scarce. It produces the black pepper tree, the leaves of which resemble those of the Sichuan pepper. It also produces the frankincense tree, the leaves of which resemble those of the flowering pear. The climate is hot, and there is much wind and dust. The nature of the people is shallow and fickle; they value wealth and despise virtue. Their script, language, customs, and laws are largely the same as those of the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國). Most do not believe in merit, and even among those who do, they revere and serve the heavenly deities. There are more than ten temples, where various heterodox sects dwell together.

zh: 從摩臘婆國西北行三日，至契吒國（南印度境）。契吒國，周三千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里。人戶殷盛，家室富饒。無大君長，役屬摩臘婆國，風土物產，遂同其俗。伽藍十餘所，僧徒千餘人，大小二乘，兼功習學。天祠數十，外道眾多。
en_current: Traveling northwest from the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國) for three days, one reaches the country of Kaṭṭa (契吒國) (within the borders of South India). The country of Kaṭṭa is more than three thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is over twenty *li* in circuit. The population is dense, and the households are wealthy. There is no great sovereign; it is subject to the country of Mālava, and its climate, products, and customs are consequently the same as that country. There are more than ten monasteries and over one thousand monks, who study both the Great and Small Vehicles with equal diligence. There are several dozen *deva* temples, and the non-Buddhists are numerous.

zh: 從此北行千餘里，至伐臘毘國（即比羅羅國。南印度境）。伐臘毘國，周六千餘里。國大都城周三十餘里。土地所產，氣序所宜，風俗人性，同摩臘婆國。居人殷盛，家室富饒，積財百億者乃有百餘室矣。遠方奇貨，多聚其國。伽藍百餘所，僧徒六千餘人，多學小乘正量部法。天祠數百，異道寔多。如來在世，屢遊此國，故無憂王於佛所止，皆樹旌表，建窣堵波。過去三佛坐及經行說法之處，遺迹相間。今王，剎帝利種也，即昔摩臘婆國尸羅阿迭多王之姪，今羯若鞠闍國尸羅阿迭多王之子婿，號杜魯婆跋吒（唐言常叡）。情性躁急，智謀淺近。然而淳信三寶，歲設大會七日，以殊珍上味，供養僧眾。三衣醫藥之價，七寶奇貴之珍，既以總施，倍價酬贖。貴德尚賢，遵道重學，遠方高僧，特加禮敬。去城不遠，有大伽藍，阿折羅阿羅漢之所建立，德慧、堅慧菩薩之所遊止，於中制論，竝盛流布。
en_current: From here, traveling north for more than one thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Valabhī (伐臘毘國) (also called the country of Bīlala; it is within the borders of Southern India). The country of Valabhī is more than six thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is more than thirty *li* in circuit. The produce of the land, the suitability of the climate, and the customs and human nature of the people are the same as in the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國). The inhabitants are prosperous, and the households are wealthy; there are more than one hundred families who have accumulated wealth of a hundred *koṭi*s. Rare goods from distant regions are mostly gathered in this country. There are more than one hundred *saṃghārāma*s, with more than six thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are several hundred *deva* temples, and the heterodox sects are very numerous. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled to this country; therefore, King Aśoka erected markers and built *stūpa*s at all the places where the Buddha stopped. The sites where the three past Buddhas sat, walked, and preached the Dharma are interspersed among them. The current king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is the nephew of the former King Śīlāditya of the country of Mālava and the son-in-law of the current King Śīlāditya of the country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國). His name is Dhruvabhaṭa (杜魯婆跋吒) (in the language of Tang, this means "Permanently Intelligent"). His temperament is impetuous, and his wisdom and strategy are shallow. However, he has pure faith in the Three Jewels. Every year, he holds a great assembly for seven days, offering rare treasures and superior delicacies to the community of monks. He gives away the value of the three robes and medicines, as well as rare and precious treasures of the seven kinds, and then redeems them at double their price. He values virtue and honors the worthy; he follows the Way and respects learning. He shows special reverence and respect to high-ranking monks from distant regions. Not far from the city is a great monastery (saṃghārāma) established by the Arhat Ācāra, where the Bodhisattvas Guṇamati and Sthiramati resided and composed treatises that are widely circulated.

zh: 自此西北行七百餘里，至阿難陀補羅國（西印度境）。阿難陀補羅國，周二千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里。人戶殷盛，家室富饒。無大君長，役屬摩臘婆國。土宜氣序，文字法則，遂亦同焉。伽藍十餘所，僧徒減千人，習學小乘正量部法。天祠數十，異道雜居。
en_current: From here, traveling northwest for over seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Ānandapura (in the territory of Western India). The country of Ānandapura is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. The population is dense and the households are wealthy. There is no great sovereign, and it is subject to the country of Mālava. The soil, climate, and the rules of writing are also the same as there. There are more than ten sanghārāmas, with fewer than one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are several dozen deva temples, where followers of various paths live together.

zh: 從伐臘毘國西行五百餘里，至蘇剌侘國（西印度境）。蘇剌侘國，周四千餘里。國大都城周三十餘里，西據莫醯河。居人殷盛，家產富饒。役屬伐臘毘國。地土鹹鹵，花菓希少。寒暑雖均，風飄不靜。土俗澆薄，人性輕躁。不好學藝，邪正兼信。伽藍五十餘所，僧徒三千餘人，多學大乘上座部法。天祠百餘所，異道雜居。國當西海之路，人皆資海之利，興販為業，貿遷有無。
en_current: Traveling westward from the kingdom of Valabhī (伐臘毘國) for over five hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Suraṭṭha (蘇剌侘國) (in the territory of Western India). The kingdom of Suraṭṭha is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the kingdom is over thirty li in circuit and borders the Mahī River (莫醯河) to the west. The inhabitants are numerous and their households are wealthy. It is subject to the kingdom of Valabhī. The land is saline and alkaline, and flowers and fruits are scarce. Although the cold and heat are balanced, the wind blows incessantly. The local customs are shallow and the people’s temperament is impulsive. They do not care for learning arts, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are over fifty saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with more than three thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. There are over one hundred deva temples, where various non-Buddhist sects dwell together. As the country lies on the route to the Western Sea, the people all rely on the benefits of the sea, engaging in trade as their profession and exchanging goods to supply what is lacking.

zh: 去城不遠，有郁鄯多山。頂有伽藍，房宇廊廡，多疏崖嶺。林樹欝茂，泉流交境，聖賢之所遊止，靈仙之所集往。
en_current: Not far from the city is Mount Ujjanta (郁鄯多山). On its summit is a monastery, with rooms and corridors mostly carved out of the cliffs and ridges. The forests and trees are lush and dense, and streams flow across the landscape; it is a place where sages and saints wander and dwell, and where spirits and immortals gather.

zh: 從伐臘毘國北行千八百餘里，至瞿折羅國（西印度境）。瞿折羅國，周五千餘里。國大都城號毘羅摩羅，周三十餘里。土宜風俗，同蘇剌侘國。居人殷盛，家產富饒。多事外道，少信佛法。伽藍一所，僧百餘人，習學小乘教說一切有部。天祠數十，異道雜居。王，剎帝利種也，年在弱冠，智勇高遠，深信佛法，高尚異能。
en_current: Traveling north from the country of Valabhī (伐臘毘國) for more than 1,800 li, one reaches the country of Gūrjara (瞿折羅國) (in the region of Western India). The country of Gūrjara is more than 5,000 li in circuit. The capital city is named Bhīlamāla (毘羅摩羅), and it is more than 30 li in circuit. The soil, climate, and customs are the same as those of the country of Surāṣṭra (蘇剌侘國). The inhabitants are prosperous, and their households are wealthy. They mostly serve non-Buddhist paths and have little faith in the Buddha’s teachings. There is one monastery with more than 100 monks, who study the teachings of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) according to the Sarvāstivāda school. There are several dozen Deva temples where followers of various non-Buddhist paths live together. The king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is in the prime of his youth, his wisdom and courage are far-reaching, he deeply believes in the Buddha’s teachings, and he holds noble and extraordinary talents in high regard.

zh: 從此東南行二千八百餘里，至鄔闍衍那國（南印度境）。鄔闍衍那國，周六千餘里。國大都城周三十餘里。土宜風俗，同蘇剌侘國。居人殷盛，家室富饒。伽藍數十所，多以圮壞，存者三五。僧徒三百餘人，大小二乘，兼功習學。天祠數十，異道雜居。王，婆羅門種也，博覽邪書，不信正法。去城不遠有窣堵波，無憂王作地獄之處。
en_current: Traveling southeast from here for over 2,800 li, one reaches the country of Ujjayanī (鄔闍衍那國) (in the territory of South India). The country of Ujjayanī is over 6,000 li in circuit. The capital city is over 30 li in circuit. The soil, climate, and customs are the same as those of the country of Surāṣṭra (蘇剌侘國). The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and the families are wealthy. There are several dozen saṃghārāmas, most of which are dilapidated, with only three or five remaining in use. There are over 300 monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles. There are several dozen Deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. The king is of the Brāhmaṇa caste; he is widely read in heterodox texts and does not believe in the true Dharma. Not far from the city is a stūpa, which is the site where King Aśoka created a hell.

zh: 從此東北行千餘里，至擲枳陀國（南印度境）。擲枳陀國，周四千餘里。國大都城周十五六里。土稱沃壤，稼穡滋植，宜菽、麥，多華菓。氣序調暢，人性善順。多信外道，少敬佛法。伽藍數十，少有僧徒。天祠十餘所，外道千餘人。王，婆羅門種也，篤信三寶，尊重有德，諸方博達之士，多集此國。
en_current: Traveling northeast from here for more than a thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Zhizhituo (擲枳陀國) (within the borders of South India). The country of Zhizhituo is more than four thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is fifteen or sixteen *li* in circuit. The soil is described as fertile, and the crops are abundant; it is suitable for beans and wheat, and there are many flowers and fruits. The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the people are gentle and compliant by nature. They mostly believe in non-Buddhist paths and have little respect for the Buddhadharma. There are several dozen *saṃghārāmas* (monasteries), but few monks. There are more than ten *deva* temples, and over a thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths. The king is of the Brahmin caste; he is a devout believer in the Three Jewels and holds virtuous people in high esteem, so many learned scholars from various regions gather in this country.

zh: 從此北行九百餘里，至摩醯濕伐羅補羅國（中印度境）。摩醯濕伐羅補羅國，周三千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里。土宜風俗，同鄔闍衍那國。宗敬外道，不信佛法。天祠數十，多是塗灰之侶。王，婆羅門種也。不甚敬信佛法。
en_current: From here, traveling northward for more than nine hundred li, one reaches the country of Maheśvarapura (in the region of Central India). The country of Maheśvarapura is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Ujjayanī (鄔闍衍那國). They revere and honor non-Buddhist paths and do not believe in the Buddha-Dharma. There are several dozen Deva temples, most of them belonging to followers who smear themselves with ash. The king is of the Brahmin caste and does not have much faith or respect for the Buddha-Dharma.

zh: 從此還至瞿折羅國，復北行荒野險磧，經千九百餘里，渡信度大河，至信度國（西印度境）。信度國，周七千餘里。國大都城號毘苫婆補羅，周三十餘里。宜穀稼，豐宿麥，出金、銀、鍮石，宜牛、羊、橐駝、騾畜之屬。橐駝卑小，唯有一峯。多出赤鹽，色如赤石，白鹽、黑鹽及白石鹽等，異域遠方以之為藥。人性剛烈而質直，數鬪諍，多誹讟。學不好博，深信佛法。伽藍數百所，僧徒萬餘人，竝學小乘正量部法，大抵懈怠，性行弊穢；其有精勤賢善之徒，獨處閑寂，遠迹山林，夙夜匪懈，多證聖果。天祠三十餘所，異道雜居。王，戍陀羅種也，性淳質，敬佛法。如來在昔頗遊此國，故無憂王於聖迹處建窣堵波數十所。烏波毱多大阿羅漢屢遊此國，演法開導，所止之處，皆旌遺迹，或建僧伽藍，或樹窣堵波，往往間起，可略而言。信度河側千餘里陂澤間，有數百千戶，於此宅居，其性剛烈，唯殺是務。牧牛自活，無所係命。若男若女，無貴無賤，剃鬚髮，服袈裟，像類苾芻，而行俗事，專執小見，非斥大乘。聞諸先志曰：昔此地民庶安忍，但事凶殘。時有羅漢愍其顛墜，為化彼故，乘虛而來，現大神通，示希有事，令眾信受，漸導言教。諸人敬悅，願奉指誨。羅漢知眾心順，為授三歸，息其兇暴，悉斷生殺，剃髮染衣，恭行法教。年代浸遠，世易時移，守善既虧，餘風不殄，雖服法衣，嘗無戒善。子孫奕世，習以成俗。
en_current: From here I returned to the country of Gurjara (瞿折羅國), then traveled north through wild wastes and dangerous deserts for over one thousand nine hundred li, crossed the great Sindhu (信度) River, and arrived at the country of Sindhu (in the territory of Western India). The country of Sindhu is over seven thousand li in circuit. The capital city is named Viṣambhapura (毘苫婆補羅), and it is over thirty li in circuit. The land is suitable for grain crops and is abundant in winter wheat; it produces gold, silver, and brass, and is suitable for raising cattle, sheep, camels, and mules. The camels are small and have only one hump. It produces much red salt, the color of which is like red stone, as well as white salt, black salt, and white rock salt; people in distant foreign lands use these as medicine. The people are fierce and straightforward by nature, frequently quarrel, and are prone to slander. They are not widely learned, but they deeply believe in the Buddhadharma. There are several hundred monasteries with over ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sammitīya school of the Hīnayāna; for the most part, they are indolent, and their character and conduct are corrupt. However, those who are diligent, virtuous, and good dwell alone in quiet seclusion, withdrawing far into the mountains and forests, and, working day and night without slackening, many attain the holy fruits. There are over thirty Deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. The king is of the Śūdra caste; he is pure and simple by nature and respects the Buddhadharma. In the past, the Tathāgata traveled extensively in this country, and therefore King Aśoka built several dozen stūpas at the sites of the holy traces. The great arhat Upagupta (烏波毱多) frequently traveled to this country to preach the Dharma and provide guidance. At every place he stayed, he marked the sacred traces, either by building a monastery (saṃghārāma) or erecting a stūpa; these rise up here and there, and can be briefly described. Along the side of the Sindhu River (信度河), in the midst of marshes extending over a thousand li, there are several hundred thousand households residing there. Their nature is fierce and violent, and they are devoted solely to killing. They herd cattle to sustain their lives and have no other means of livelihood. Whether male or female, noble or base, they shave their hair and beards and wear the kaṣāya (monastic robes), appearing like bhikṣus while engaging in secular affairs; they stubbornly hold to narrow views and reject the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). I have heard from the records of the ancients: "In the past, the common people of this land were hardened and cruel, devoted only to violence." At that time, an arhat took pity on their fallen state and, in order to transform them, came through the void, manifesting great supernatural powers and displaying rare wonders, causing the multitude to believe and accept his teachings, which he introduced gradually. The people were respectful and pleased, and wished to follow his instructions. The arhat, knowing that the hearts of the multitude were compliant, administered the three refuges to them, calmed their ferocity, caused them to completely cease killing, and had them shave their hair, dye their garments, and respectfully practice the teachings of the Dharma. As the ages grew distant and the world changed with the passage of time, their adherence to goodness faltered, yet the remnants of their old customs were not extinguished; although they wear the robes of the Dharma, they have never possessed the precepts or virtue. Their descendants, generation after generation, have made this their custom.

zh: 從此東行九百餘里，渡信度河東岸，至茂羅三部盧國（西印度境）。茂羅三部盧國，周四千餘里。國大都城周三十餘里。居人殷盛，家室富饒。役屬磔迦國。土田良沃，氣序調順。風俗質直，好學尚德。多事天神，少信佛法。伽藍十餘所，多已圮壞，少有僧徒，學無專習。天祠八所，異道雜居。有日天祠，莊嚴甚麗，其日天像鑄以黃金，飾以奇寶。靈鑒幽通，神功潛被，女樂遞奏，明炬繼日，香花供養，初無廢絕。五印度國諸王豪族，莫不於此捨施珍寶，建立福舍，以飲食醫藥給濟貧病。諸國之人來此求願，常有千數，天祠四周，池沼花林，甚可遊賞。
en_current: From here, traveling east for over nine hundred li and crossing to the eastern bank of the Indus River (Sindhu), one arrives at the country of Mūlasthānapura (茂羅三部盧國) (in the region of Western India). The country of Mūlasthānapura is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is over thirty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and the households are wealthy. It is subject to the country of Takka (磔迦國). The land is fertile and productive, and the climate is temperate and regular. The customs of the people are honest and straightforward; they are fond of learning and value virtue. They mostly serve the heavenly deities and have little faith in the Buddha-dharma. There are more than ten sanghārāmas, most of which are dilapidated; there are few monks, and they do not specialize in any particular study. There are eight deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths live together. There is a Temple of the Sun God, which is extremely magnificent and beautiful; the image of the Sun God is cast in gold and adorned with rare jewels. Its spiritual influence is profound and mysterious, and its divine efficacy is secretly bestowed. Female musicians play in rotation, bright torches burn continuously day and night, and offerings of incense and flowers are never interrupted. The kings and noble families of the five Indias never fail to donate precious treasures here and establish charitable houses to provide food, drink, and medicine to the poor and the sick. People from various countries come here to offer prayers, often numbering in the thousands. Around the deva temple, the ponds and flowery woods are most pleasant for sightseeing.

zh: 從此東北行七百餘里，至鉢伐多國（北印度境）。鉢伐多國，周五千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里。居人殷盛。役屬磔迦國。多早稻，宜宿、麥。氣序調適，風俗質直，人性躁急，言含鄙辭。學藝深博，邪正雜信。伽藍十餘所，僧徒千餘人。大小二乘，兼功習學。四窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。天祠二十，異道雜居。城側有大伽藍，僧徒百餘人，並學大乘教，即是昔慎那弗呾羅（唐言最勝子）論師於此製《瑜伽師地釋論》，亦是賢愛論師、德光論師本出家處。此大伽藍為天火所燒，摧殘荒圮。
en_current: From here, traveling northeast for more than seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Parvata (鉢伐多國) (within the borders of Northern India). The country of Parvata is more than five thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are prosperous and numerous. It is subject to the country of Takka (磔迦國). There is much early-ripening rice, and it is suitable for winter wheat. The climate is temperate, the customs are simple and honest, the people’s temperament is impetuous and hasty, and their speech contains vulgar expressions. They are deeply learned in the arts and sciences, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks, who study both the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings. There are four stūpas, which were built by King Aśoka. There are twenty Deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Beside the city is a large monastery with over a hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahayana teachings; this is where the former śāstra master Jinaputra (in Chinese, "Most Victorious Son" (最勝子)) composed the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā*, and it is also the place where the śāstra masters Bhadraruci and Guṇaprabha originally entered the monastic order. This large monastery was burned by celestial fire and is now ruined and desolate.

zh: 從信度國西南行千五六百里，至阿點婆翅羅國（西印度境）。阿點婆翅羅國，周五千餘里。國大都城號朅䶩濕伐羅，周三十餘里。僻在西境，臨信度河，隣大海濱。屋宇莊嚴，多有珍寶。近無君長，統屬信度國。地下濕，土斥鹵，穢草荒茂，疇壟少墾，穀稼雖備，宿、麥特豐。氣序微寒，風飈勁烈。宜牛、羊、橐駝、騾畜之類。人性暴急，不好習學。語言微異中印度。其俗淳質，敬崇三寶。伽藍八十餘所，僧徒五千餘人，多學小乘正量部法。天祠十所，多是塗灰外道之所居止。城中有大自在天祠。祠宇彫飾，天像靈鑒，塗灰外道遊舍其中。在昔如來頗遊此國，說法度人，導凡利俗，故無憂王於聖迹處建六窣堵波焉。
en_current: Traveling southwest from the country of Sindhu (信度國) for fifteen or sixteen hundred li, one reaches the country of Audumbatira (阿點婆翅羅國) (within the borders of West India). The country of Audumbatira is over five thousand li in circuit. The great capital city is named Khasvara (朅䶩濕伐羅), and it is over thirty li in circuit. It is situated in a remote western region, bordering the Sindhu River and adjacent to the shore of the great sea. The buildings are magnificent and contain many precious treasures. Recently, it has had no sovereign and is under the jurisdiction of the country of Sindhu. The ground is low and damp, the soil is saline, and foul weeds grow in abundance. The fields are little cultivated; although all types of grain are present, winter wheat is particularly abundant. The climate is slightly cold, and the winds are fierce and strong.
