The King of Kustana (瞿薩旦那), moved by the great kindness of the rats, built a shrine and established sacrifices, a tradition of reverence followed for generations with profound and special esteem. Therefore, from the monarch above to the common people below, all perform sacrifices to seek blessings and protection. When passing by their burrows, people alight from their mounts and hurry forward, bowing to pay their respects and offering sacrifices to pray for good fortune. Whether offering clothing, bows, and arrows, or fragrant flowers and fine foods, once they have shown their sincerity, they mostly receive benefits and blessings. If they fail to offer sacrifices, they encounter disasters and calamities.

zh: 王城西五六里，有娑摩若僧伽藍。中有窣堵波，高百餘尺，甚多靈瑞，時燭神光。昔有羅漢，自遠方來，止此林中，以神通力，放大光明。時王夜在重閣，遙見林中光明照曜，於是歷問，僉曰：「有一沙門，自遠而至，宴坐林中，示現神通。」王遂命駕，躬往觀察。既覩明賢，乃心祗敬，欽風不已，請至中宮。沙門曰：「物有所宜，志其所在。幽林藪澤，情之所賞；高堂邃宇，非我攸聞。」王益敬仰，深加宗重，為建伽藍，起窣堵波。沙門受請，遂止其中。頃之，王感獲舍利數百粒，甚慶悅，竊自念曰：「舍利來應，何其晚歟？早得置之窣堵波下，豈非勝迹？」尋詣伽藍，具白沙門。羅漢曰：「王無憂也，今為置之。宜以金、銀、銅、鐵大石函等，以次周盛。」王命匠人，不日功畢，載諸寶輿，送至伽藍。是時也，王宮導從、庶僚凡百，觀送舍利者，動以萬計。羅漢乃以右手舉窣堵波，置諸掌中，謂王曰：「可以藏下也。」遂坎地安函，其功斯畢，於是下窣堵波，無所傾損。觀覩之徒，歎未曾有，信佛之心彌篤，敬法之志斯堅。王謂群官曰：「我嘗聞佛力難思，神通難究。或分身百億，或應迹人天；舉世界於掌內，眾生無動靜之想，演法性於常音，眾生有隨類之悟。斯則神力不共，智慧絕言。其靈已隱，其教猶傳。飡和飲澤，味道欽風，尚獲斯靈，深賴其福。勉哉，凡百！宜深崇敬，佛法幽深，於是明矣。」
en_current: Five or six li to the west of the royal city is the Samājña Monastery (娑摩若僧伽藍). Within it is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, which possesses many miraculous signs and often illuminates with divine light. Formerly, there was an arhat who came from a distant land and stayed in this forest, manifesting great light through his supernatural powers. At that time, the king was in his multi-storied pavilion at night and saw from afar the light shining in the forest. He inquired about it, and everyone said, "There is a śramaṇa who has arrived from afar, sitting in meditation in the forest and manifesting supernatural powers." The king then ordered his carriage and went in person to observe. Having seen the wise and virtuous one, he felt deep respect and admiration for his character, and invited him to the royal palace. The śramaṇa said, "Things have their proper places, and one’s aspirations lie where they belong. Secluded forests and marshes are what my heart delights in; high halls and deep chambers are not what I am accustomed to." The king respected and revered him all the more, and for his sake built a monastery and erected a stūpa. The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and subsequently resided there. Shortly after, the king miraculously obtained several hundred grains of relics. He was extremely joyful and thought to himself, "Why did the relics come to respond so late? If I had obtained them earlier to place them under the stūpa, would that not have been a magnificent monument?" He immediately went to the monastery and told the śramaṇa in detail. The arhat said, "O King, do not worry; I shall place them for you now. You should use caskets of gold, silver, copper, iron, and large stone, one inside the other, to contain them." The king ordered the craftsmen, and in a few days the work was completed. He loaded them onto a precious carriage and sent them to the monastery. At that time, the king’s royal retinue and the various officials, numbering in the tens of thousands, came to witness the sending of the relics. The arhat then lifted the stūpa with his right hand, placed it in his palm, and said to the king, "You may now bury them beneath it." Thereupon, a pit was dug in the ground and the caskets were installed. When the task was finished, the stūpa was lowered back down without any tilting or damage. Those who witnessed it marveled that such a thing had never happened before; their faith in the Buddha became even more sincere, and their resolve to revere the Dharma grew more steadfast.  The king said to his officials, "I have heard that the power of the Buddha is inconceivable and his supernatural faculties are unfathomable. Sometimes he manifests billions of bodies, and sometimes he leaves traces of his presence among humans and devas. He can lift the entire world into the palm of his hand without the sentient beings within it having any sense of movement or stillness; he expounds the nature of the Dharma in a constant sound, and sentient beings attain understanding according to their own kind. This is the uncommon power of his supernatural faculties and wisdom that transcends words. Though his spiritual presence has vanished, his teachings are still transmitted. By consuming his harmony and drinking his grace, by savoring the Way and admiring his influence, we still obtain such spiritual efficacy and rely deeply upon his blessings. Exert yourselves, all of you! You should offer deep veneration; that the Buddha-dharma is abstruse and profound is evident from this."

zh: 王城東南五六里，有麻射僧伽藍，此國先王妃所立也。昔者，此國未知桑蠶，聞東國有也，命使以求。時東國君祕而不賜，嚴勅關防，無令桑蠶種出也。瞿薩旦那王乃卑辭下禮，求婚東國；國君有懷遠之志，遂允其請。瞿薩旦那王命使迎婦，而誡曰：「爾致辭東國君女，我國素無絲綿桑蠶之種，可以持來，自為裳服。」女聞其言，密求其種，以桑蠶之子置帽絮中，既至關防，主者遍索，唯王女帽不敢以驗。遂入瞿薩旦那國，止麻射伽藍故地，方備儀禮，奉迎入宮，以桑蠶種留於此地。陽春告始，乃植其桑，蠶月既臨，復事採養。初至也，尚以雜葉𩚅之，自時厥後，桑樹連陰。王妃乃刻石為制，不令傷殺；蠶蛾飛盡，乃得治繭。敢有犯違，明神不祐。遂為先蠶建此伽藍。數株枯桑，云是本種之樹也。故今此國有蠶不殺，竊有取絲者，來年輒不宜蠶。
en_current: Five or six li southeast of the royal city is the Ma-ża (麻射) Monastery, which was established by a former queen of this country. In ancient times, this country did not know of mulberry trees or silkworms. Hearing that they existed in the eastern country, the king sent an envoy to request them. At that time, the ruler of the eastern country kept them secret and would not bestow them, strictly ordering the frontier guards not to allow the seeds of mulberry or silkworms to pass out. The King of Gostana (瞿薩旦那國) then used humble words and low courtesies to request a marriage alliance with the eastern country. The ruler of that country, having a desire to extend his influence to distant lands, granted the request. The King of Gostana ordered an envoy to receive the bride and instructed him, saying: "Convey this message to the daughter of the eastern ruler: our country has never had silk, floss, or the seeds of mulberry and silkworms; she may bring them with her so that she may make her own garments." Upon hearing these words, the princess secretly sought the seeds and placed the silkworm eggs inside the padding of her hat. When she reached the frontier, the officials searched everywhere, but they did not dare to inspect the princess's hat. She then entered the country of Gostana and stopped at the former site of the Ma-ża Monastery. Only after the proper rites and ceremonies were prepared was she escorted into the palace, and the mulberry and silkworm seeds were left at this location. When the warmth of spring began, she planted the mulberry trees, and when the silkworm month arrived, she proceeded to gather and raise them. When they first arrived, she still fed them with various leaves, but from that time on, the mulberry trees grew in continuous shade. The queen then had a decree carved into stone, forbidding their injury or killing; only after the silkworm moths had flown away could the cocoons be processed. Anyone who dared to violate this would not be protected by the bright spirits. She then built this monastery for the first silkworms. Several withered mulberry trees are said to be the trees of the original stock. Therefore, in this country today, silkworms are not killed; if anyone stealthily takes their silk, the sericulture will surely be unsuccessful the following year.

zh: 池側伽藍，荒圮無僧。
en_current: The monastery beside the pond is deserted and in ruins, with no monks residing there.

zh: 城東南百餘里有大河，西北流，國人利之，以用溉田。其後斷流，王深怪異。於是命駕問羅漢僧曰：「大河之水，國人取給，今忽斷流，其咎安在？為政有不平，德有不洽乎？不然，垂譴何重也？」羅漢曰：「大王治國，政化清和。河水斷流，龍所為耳。宜速祠求，當復昔利。」王因迴駕，祠祭河龍。忽有一女凌波而至，曰：「我夫早喪，主命無從；所以河水絕流，農人失利。王於國內選一貴臣，配我為夫，水流如昔。」王曰：「敬聞，任所欲耳。」龍遂目悅國之大臣。王既迴駕，謂群下曰：「大臣者，國之重鎮；農務者，人之命食。國失鎮則危，人絕食則死。危、死之事，何所宜行？」大臣越席，跪而對曰：「久已虛薄，謬當重任。常思報國，未遇其時，今而預選，敢塞深責。苟利萬姓，何吝一臣？臣者，國之佐；人者，國之本，願大王不再思也。幸為修福，建僧伽藍。」王允所求，功成不日。其臣又請早入龍宮，於是舉國僚庶，鼓樂飲餞。其臣乃衣素服，乘白馬，與王辭訣，敬謝國人。驅馬入河，履水不溺，濟乎中流，麾鞭畫水，水為中開，自茲沒矣。頃之，白馬浮出，負一栴檀大鼓，封一函書。其書大略曰：「大王不遺細微，謬參神選，願多營福，益國滋臣。以此大鼓，懸城東南，若有寇至，鼓先聲震。」河水遂流，至今利用。歲月浸遠，龍鼓久無。舊懸之處，今仍有鼓。
en_current: More than a hundred li to the southeast of the city is a large river flowing northwest; the people of the country benefit from it, using it to irrigate their fields. Later, the flow ceased, and the king was deeply puzzled and alarmed. He then ordered his carriage and went to ask an Arhat (阿羅漢) monk, saying: "The water of the great river is what the people rely on for their needs; now that it has suddenly stopped flowing, where does the fault lie? Is my governance unjust, or is my virtue not in harmony? If not, why is this reprimand so severe?" The Arhat said: "Great King, your governance of the country is clear and harmonious. The river's flow has ceased because of the dragon. You should quickly offer sacrifices and pray, and the former benefits will return." The king then returned and offered sacrifices to the river dragon. Suddenly, a woman arrived, walking upon the waves, and said: "My husband died early, and I have no one to follow; this is why the river's flow has ceased and the farmers have lost their livelihood. If the King selects a noble minister from within the country to be my husband, the water will flow as before." The king said: "I respectfully hear your request; it is for you to choose whom you desire." The dragon then cast her eyes upon a high minister of the country. The king, having returned, said to his subordinates: "A high minister is the heavy pillar of the state; agricultural work is the life-sustaining food of the people. If the state loses its pillar, it is in danger; if the people are cut off from food, they die. Regarding these matters of danger and death, what is appropriate to do?" A minister stepped across his mat, knelt, and replied: "I have long been hollow and meager, yet I have mistakenly occupied a heavy responsibility. I have always thought of repaying the state, but have not yet encountered the time to do so. Now that I have been selected, how would I dare to refuse this profound duty? If it benefits the myriad people, why should I begrudge one minister?" "Ministers are the assistants of the state; the people are the foundation of the state. I hope the Great King will not hesitate further. I pray you cultivate merit and build a saṃghārāma." The King granted his request, and the work was completed in a few days. The minister then requested to enter the dragon palace early. Thereupon, the officials and commoners of the entire country played music and held a farewell feast. The minister donned plain white garments, mounted a white horse, bade farewell to the King, and respectfully thanked the people of the country. He urged his horse into the river, treading upon the water without sinking. Upon reaching midstream, he brandished his whip and traced a line on the water; the water parted in the middle, and he vanished from there. After a short while, the white horse floated to the surface, carrying a large sandalwood drum and a sealed letter. The letter said in brief: "Your Majesty did not overlook my humble status and allowed me to be mistakenly chosen by the divine; I hope you will perform many meritorious deeds to benefit the state and nourish your subjects. Take this large drum and hang it to the southeast of the city; if invaders approach, the drum will sound a warning first." The river water then flowed on, and it remains useful to this day. As the years and months have passed, the dragon drum has long been gone, but at the place where it was formerly hung, there is still a drum today.

zh: 王城東三百餘里大荒澤中，數十頃地，絕無櫱草，其土赤黑。聞諸耆舊曰：敗軍之地也。昔者，東國軍師百萬西伐，此時瞿薩旦那王亦整齊戎馬數十萬眾，東禦強敵，至於此地，兩軍相遇，因即合戰。西兵失利，乘勝殘殺，虜其王，殺其將，誅戮士卒，無復孑遺。流血染地，其迹斯在。
en_current: More than three hundred *li* to the east of the royal city, in the midst of a vast marsh, there is an area of several tens of *qing* where no vegetation grows and the soil is reddish-black. According to the elders, this is the place of a defeated army. In the past, an eastern country raised a million troops to invade the west. At that time, the King of Gostana (瞿薩旦那) also prepared hundreds of thousands of soldiers to resist the powerful enemy from the east. When the two armies met at this place, they immediately engaged in battle. The western army suffered defeat, and the victors, taking advantage of their success, slaughtered them cruelly, capturing their king, killing their generals, and massacring the soldiers until not a single one remained. The blood shed stained the ground, and the traces are still visible there.

zh: 戰地東行三十餘里，至嫓摩城。有彫檀立佛像，高二丈餘。甚多靈應，時燭光明。凡有疾病，隨其痛處，金薄帖像，即時痊復，虛心請願，多亦遂求。聞之土俗曰：此像，昔佛在世憍賞彌國鄔陀衍那王所作也。佛去世後，自彼凌空至此國北曷勞落迦城中。初到此，城人安樂富饒，深著邪見，而不珍敬，傳其自來，神而不貴。後有羅漢禮拜此像，國人驚駭，異其容服，馳以白王。王乃下令，宜以沙土坌此異人。時阿羅漢身蒙沙土，餬口絕糧。時有一人，心甚不忍，昔常恭敬尊禮此像，及見羅漢，密以饌之。羅漢將去，謂其人曰：「却後七日，當雨沙土，填滿此城，略無遺類。爾宜知之，早圖出計。猶其坌我，獲斯殃耳。」語已便去，忽然不見。其人入城，具告親故，或有聞者，莫不嗤笑。至第二日，大風忽發，吹去穢壤，雨雜寶滿衢路，人更罵所告者。此人心知必然，竊開孔道，出城外而穴之。第七日夜，宵分之後，雨沙土滿城中。其人從孔道出，東趣此國，止嫓摩城。其人纔至，其像亦來，即此供養，不敢遷移。聞諸先記曰：釋迦法盡，像入龍宮。今曷勞落迦城為大堆阜，諸國君王、異方豪右，多欲發掘，取其寶物。適至其側，猛風暴發，煙雲四合，道路迷失。
en_current: Traveling more than thirty *li* east from the battlefield, one arrives at the city of Pimo (媲摩城). There is a standing sandalwood Buddha image over two *zhang* in height. It possesses many miraculous powers and at times emits a brilliant light. Whenever people have illnesses, they apply gold leaf to the part of the image corresponding to their own area of pain, and they are immediately cured. Those who make requests with a sincere heart often have their wishes fulfilled. I heard the local people say: "This image was made by King Udayana (鄔陀衍那王) of the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國) when the Buddha was still in the world. After the Buddha passed away, it traveled through the air from there to the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) in the north of this country." When it first arrived, the people of the city were peaceful and prosperous, but they were deeply attached to erroneous views and did not treasure or respect it; although they heard it had come of its own accord, they considered it divine but did not value it. Later, an Arhat came to pay homage to this image. The people of the city were shocked, finding his appearance and clothing strange, and they rushed to inform the king. The king then issued an order that this strange man should be covered with sand and earth. At that time, the Arhat was covered in sand and earth, his mouth blocked and his food supply cut off. There was one man whose heart could not bear this; he had long held this image in reverent worship, and upon seeing the Arhat, he secretly provided him with food. When the Arhat was about to depart, he said to the man: "Seven days from now, it will rain sand and earth, filling this city until not a single soul remains. You should know this and plan your escape early. It is because they covered me with sand that they have brought this calamity upon themselves." Having spoken, he departed and suddenly vanished. The man entered the city and told his relatives and friends in detail, but those who heard him did nothing but laugh and mock him. On the second day, a great wind suddenly arose, blowing away the filth and soil, and it rained various treasures that filled the streets; the people then berated their informant even more. This man, knowing in his heart that it was inevitable, secretly opened a tunnel, exited the city, and took shelter outside. On the night of the seventh day, after midnight, sand and earth rained down and filled the city. The man emerged from the tunnel and went east to this country, staying in the city of Bhīmā (嫓摩城). No sooner had the man arrived than the image also arrived; he immediately worshipped it there and dared not move it. According to ancient records, when the Dharma of Śākyamuni comes to an end, the image will enter the dragon palace. Today, the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) has become a great mound. Kings of various nations and powerful men from distant lands have often desired to excavate it to take its treasures, but as soon as they reach its vicinity, fierce winds suddenly arise, smoke and clouds gather from all sides, and the roads become lost.

zh: 佛去世後，自彼凌空至此國北曷勞落迦城中。初到此，城人安樂富饒，深著邪見，而不珍敬，傳其自來，神而不貴。後有羅漢禮拜此像，國人驚駭，異其容服，馳以白王。王乃下令，宜以沙土坌此異人。時阿羅漢身蒙沙土，餬口絕糧。時有一人，心甚不忍，昔常恭敬尊禮此像，及見羅漢，密以饌之。羅漢將去，謂其人曰：「却後七日，當雨沙土，填滿此城，略無遺類。爾宜知之，早圖出計。猶其坌我，獲斯殃耳。」語已便去，忽然不見。其人入城，具告親故，或有聞者，莫不嗤笑。至第二日，大風忽發，吹去穢壤，雨雜寶滿衢路，人更罵所告者。此人心知必然，竊開孔道，出城外而穴之。第七日夜，宵分之後，雨沙土滿城中。其人從孔道出，東趣此國，止嫓摩城。其人纔至，其像亦來，即此供養，不敢遷移。聞諸先記曰：釋迦法盡，像入龍宮。今曷勞落迦城為大堆阜，諸國君王、異方豪右，多欲發掘，取其寶物。適至其側，猛風暴發，煙雲四合，道路迷失。
en_current: After the Buddha had passed away, [the image] traveled through the air from that place to the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) in the north of this country. When it first arrived, the people of the city were peaceful and prosperous, but they were deeply attached to wrong views and did not value or respect it; they passed on the story of its arrival, regarding it as a spirit but not holding it in high esteem. Later, an Arhat came to pay homage to this image. The people of the country were shocked, finding his appearance and robes strange, and they rushed to inform the king. The king then issued an order that this strange man should be covered with sand and earth. At that time, the Arhat’s body was covered in sand and earth, and he was deprived of food and drink. There was one man whose heart could not bear this; he had previously always respectfully honored this image, and upon seeing the Arhat, he secretly provided him with food. When the Arhat was about to depart, he said to the man, "Seven days from now, it shall rain sand and earth, filling this city until not a single soul remains. You should know this and plan your escape early. It is because they covered me with sand that they shall meet this calamity." Having spoken, he departed and suddenly vanished. The man entered the city and told his relatives and friends in detail, but those who heard him did nothing but laugh and mock him. On the second day, a great wind suddenly arose, blowing away the filth and raining down various treasures that filled the streets; the people then further scolded the one who had warned them. This man knew in his heart that it was inevitable, so he secretly opened a tunnel, went outside the city, and took shelter there. On the night of the seventh day, after midnight, sand and earth rained down and filled the city. The man emerged from the tunnel and went east to this country, staying in the city of Bhīmā (嫓摩城). No sooner had the man arrived than the image also came; he immediately made offerings to it there and dared not move it again. According to ancient records, when the Dharma of Śākyamuni comes to an end, the image will enter the palace of the dragons. Today, the city of Rauraka (曷勞落迦城) has become a great mound. Kings of various nations and powerful men from distant lands have often desired to excavate it to take its treasures. Yet, as soon as they reach its side, a violent gale suddenly breaks out, clouds and mist close in from all sides, and they lose their way.

zh: 嫓摩川東入沙磧，行二百餘里，至尼攘城，周三四里，在大澤中。澤地熱濕，難以履涉；蘆草荒茂，無復途徑，唯趣城路，僅得通行。故往來者莫不由此城焉。而瞿薩旦那以為東境之關防也。
en_current: Going east from the Bhīmā River (嫓摩川) into the sandy desert, one travels more than two hundred li and reaches the city of Niyang (尼攘城), which is three or four li in circuit and situated in the midst of a vast marsh. The marshy ground is hot and damp, making it difficult to walk or wade; the reeds and grasses are overgrown, and there are no longer any paths, so that only the road leading to the city is passable. Therefore, all those who come and go must pass through this city. The kingdom of Gostana (瞿薩旦那) considers it a strategic frontier post for its eastern border.

zh: 從此東行入大流沙，沙則流漫，聚散隨風，人行無迹，遂多迷路。四遠茫茫，莫知所指，是以往來聚遺骸以記之。乏水草，多熱風；風起則人畜惛迷，因以成病。時聞歌嘯，或聞號哭。視聽之間，恍然不知所至，由此屢有喪亡，蓋鬼魅之所致也。行四百餘里，至都邏故國。國久空曠，城皆荒蕪。
en_current: From here, traveling east, one enters the Great Quicksand (Taklamakan Desert), where the sands shift and flow, gathering and scattering with the wind. As human footsteps leave no trace, many people lose their way. The vast expanse stretches out in all directions with no landmarks to point the way, so travelers collect the bleached bones of the dead to serve as markers. There is a lack of water and vegetation, and there are many hot winds; when the wind rises, both people and animals become dazed and confused, thereby falling ill. At times, one hears singing and whistling, or hears wailing and crying. Amidst these sights and sounds, one becomes utterly bewildered and loses all sense of direction; this has led to frequent deaths, for it is surely the work of demons and malevolent spirits. Traveling more than four hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Tu-huo-lo (都邏故國; *Tukhāra*). The country has long been empty and vast, and its cities are all desolate and overgrown.

zh: 從此東行六百餘里，至折摩馱那故國，即涅末地也。城郭巋然，人煙斷絕。
en_current: From here, traveling east for more than six hundred li, one reaches the old country of Calmadana (折摩馱那故國), which is the land of Jumo (涅末地). The city walls stand tall and solitary, but all signs of human habitation have vanished.

zh: 復此東北行千餘里，至納縛波故國，即樓蘭地也。推表山川，考採境壤，詳國俗之剛柔，繫水土之風氣，動靜無常，取捨不同，事難窮驗，非可仰說。隨所遊至，略書梗概，舉其聞見，記諸慕化。斯故日入已來，咸沐惠澤，風行所及，皆仰至德。混同天下，一之宇內，豈徒單車出使，通驛萬里者哉。
en_current: Traveling northeast from here for over a thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Navapa (納縛波故國), which is the land of Loulan (樓蘭). Regarding the mapping of mountains and rivers, the investigation of territories and soils, the detailing of the hard or soft nature of national customs, and the connection to the local climates and airs—since movement and stillness are impermanent and choices differ, these matters are difficult to verify exhaustively and cannot be explained merely by looking upward. Following where I have traveled, I have briefly written down the general outlines, citing what I have heard and seen, and recording those who admire the civilizing influence. Therefore, from the place where the sun sets, all are bathed in the grace and benevolence; wherever the wind of his influence reaches, all look up to his supreme virtue. He has unified the world and brought oneness to all within the universe; how could this be merely the act of a solitary envoy in a single carriage traveling ten thousand *li* through postal stations?

zh: 東主乘勝，撫集亡國，遷都中地，方建城郭。憂其無土，恐難成功，宣告遠近，誰識地理。時有塗灰外道，負大瓠，盛滿水，而自進曰：「我知地理。」遂以其水屈曲遺流，周而復始，因即疾驅，忽而不見。依彼水迹，峙其基堵，遂得興功，即斯國治，今王所都於此城也。城非崇峻，攻擊難剋，自古已來，未能有勝。
en_current: The Eastern Lord, taking advantage of his victory, comforted and gathered the people of the defeated state, moved the capital to the central region, and began to build city walls. He worried about the lack of soil and feared that the project might not succeed, so he made a proclamation far and near, asking who understood the geography of the land. At that time, there was an ash-smearing ascetic (pāśupata) carrying a large gourd filled with water who stepped forward and said, "I understand the geography." He then let the water flow out in winding curves, circling back to the beginning, after which he hurried away and suddenly vanished. Following those water marks, the foundations were raised and the construction was successfully undertaken; this became the seat of government, and the current king has established his capital in this city. The city is not high or steep, yet it is difficult to overcome in an attack; since ancient times, no one has ever been able to conquer it.
